utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-97-24-A, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. I see the interpreters are in their booth, and I see that Mr. Stakic is in. Mr. Stakic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Appearances for the parties. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mark McKeon for the Prosecution, together with Xavier Tracol, Barbara Goy, and our case manager, Andres Vatter. Helen Brady will be joining us later this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McKeon. Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is John Ostojic, along with Mr. Branko Lukic, we're here for Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. You may sit down. Today we will continue hearing the merits of the appeals in the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic. First we will give the Defence one hour and 30 minutes to respond to the Prosecution's submissions presented yesterday. The Prosecution will then have 20 minutes to reply, and after the reply, we will take a 30-minute break. After the break, we will continue with our proceedings. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And once again, good morning. Good morning, Appellate Chamber. May it please the Court, once again, my name is John Ostojic, and along with Mr. Lukic, we represent Milomir Stakic. I will be responding to the four matters raised on appeal by the OTP in their appeal against the trial judgement relating to genocide. Initially, we submit that each of the issues raised on appeal by the OTP should be denied and dismissed. We respectfully submit that despite the fact that they may raise issues of first impression, each and all of the issues raised do not meet the recognised standards of appellate review. The first and second grounds of appeal are allegedly based on the factual finding of the judgement within which the OTP claims consists of three legal errors. The first ground is in essence a claim that the Trial Chamber erred because it found that Dr. Stakic did not possess the dolus specialis required for genocide. The Prosecution's view and allegation is that what caused the Trial Chamber to evaluate the evidence improperly was, among other things, that it confused motive with intent. The basis for their opinion, once again, is that the Trial Chamber confused motive with intent. The Prosecution, in reliance on their theory, cites paragraph 553 of the trial judgement and the trial court's use of the term "rather" as follows. If I may just turn to paragraph 553, so I don't misstate what it says. And this begins in the second, I believe, or four lines below starting on 553, it states: "While the Chamber is satisfied that the common goal of the members of the SDS in the municipality of Prijedor, including Dr. Stakic, as president of the Municipal Assembly, was to establish a Serbian municipality, there is insufficient evidence of an intention to do so by destroying, in part, the Muslim group." The Trial Chamber then proceeds to further explain what it believes were the reasons or motives behind the common goal. The Trial Chamber itself, again at paragraph 553, states the critical word that the Prosecution seems to find so objectionable: "The Trial Chamber believes that the goal was rather to eliminate any perceived threat, especially by Muslims, to the overall plan and to force non-Serbs to leave the municipality of Prijedor." The term "rather," as used by the trial court, does not reveal or reflect, impute, or reveal that the trial court, as alleged by the OTP, confused motive with intent. In fact, we submit that the trial court extensively scrutinised all the evidence and was still unable to find dolus specialis, because it did not exist, not for the reasons alleged by the Prosecution. In fact, in the very next paragraph of the judgement, the trial court states that it was unable to infer such intent even from Dr. Stakic's use of what they coin hateful terminology. The trial court ultimately correctly concluded that the intention to displace is not equivalent to the intention to destroy. What is, in our submission, important is that the trial court, on the evidence, found that there was "insufficient evidence of an intention to do so by destroying in part the Muslim group." And that's again at paragraph 553. I stress "in part" simply because it leads to another aspect or reason of the Prosecution's purported claim for appeal. But the emphasis here is that the trial court clearly found insufficient evidence. It's the evidence that they looked at. There's no evidence other than this one word that the Prosecution claims purports to support their position that the Trial Chamber confused motive with intent. The trial court also, in other portions of their trial judgement, find at paragraph 51: "That a genocidal intent on a higher level has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt." The thoroughness of this Court to examine the specific intent and the mens rea required for genocide was indeed exhaustive. They looked at all possible levels, vertically, horizontally, as well as, if I can use this word, subordinately, below Dr. Stakic. So it found at paragraph 551, again "that a genocidal intent on a higher level has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt." Did they confuse motive and intent in that aspect? No such appeal has been raised, because there is no evidence. And quite frankly, it's not accurate to claim that there was a confusion by the use of the one word "rather." Further, the Trial Chamber notes, at paragraph 552: "That the Prosecution has explicitly stated that it has not charged Dr. Stakic with crimes when it would be necessary to prove a vertical joint criminal enterprise extending beyond Prijedor." So now we have two situations: No vertical -- no evidence of a vertical dolus specialis and no evidence of a horizontal dolus specialis. The trial court continues, and it states at paragraph 555 of the trial judgement: "While discussing horizontal level of dolus specialis for genocide and concluded there is no compelling evidence to this effect." Likewise, in our view, the trial court correctly, at page 559, considered whether subordinates of Dr. Stakic in the municipality of Prijedor had the dolus specialis for genocide. And it found and concluded, again at page 559 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I presume you are -- paragraph 559?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Thank you, Mr. President. It's paragraph 559 at page 159 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Our judgements are already long enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that. I apologise. Thank you. Once again, at paragraph 559, page 159, which I think caused some confusion with my handwriting, it states, in the second sentence: "Since the Trial Chamber is not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that anyone, including any subordinates of Dr. Stakic in the municipality of Prijedor, had the dolus specialis, there is no room for the application of Article 7(3) in relation to Count 1." Perhaps most telling is the trial judgement and its findings after reviewing all the evidence, after reviewing the horizontal level, the vertical level, and the subordinate level, it now turns specifically to Dr. Stakic. At paragraph 616, the Trial Chamber concludes, and I quote: "The Trial Chamber does not believe that the conscious object of Dr. Stakic's participation in the creation and maintenance of this environment of impunity was to kill the non-Serb citizens of Prijedor municipality." The Trial Chamber not only found that there was no vertical intent for genocide, that there was no horizontal intent for genocide, that there was no subordinate special intent for genocide. It also reasonably concluded, based on all the evidence, at paragraph 616, that Dr. Stakic himself not only did not have, in my view, the special intent to commit genocide; the Trial Chamber goes further and states that Dr. Stakic did not have the conscious object, did not have any intent to kill. They use specifically the words "to kill." That's their conclusion. You'll find hopefully in our presentation later this afternoon that we believe this is inconsistent, inherently inconsistent, with other findings and the ultimate disposition as it may relate to Dr. Stakic. But for our purposes now, we're addressing this paragraph to show that at every possible level, the trial court at no time confused motive with intent, and in fact reasonably relied on the evidence when it found unequivocally that there was no dolus specialis for genocide at either the horizontal, vertical, subordinate, or even himself, and properly acquitted Dr. Stakic of genocide. The trial court, it is respectfully submitted, was not, as alleged by the Prosecution, confused about motive and intent, but correctly found on the totality of the evidence presented that Dr. Stakic at no time, or at any time, possessed the dolus specialis for genocide to be applied. We respectfully request that the OTP's first ground of appeal, premised upon paragraph 553 of the trial judgement and the word "rather," in light of the full trial judgement and its findings specifically as to Dr. Stakic, persons vertical, horizontal, and subordinate to him, that there was insufficient evidence to establish dolus specialis warrant a dismissal of their first appeal. Within the first ground of appeal, however, the Prosecution adds another reason or basis as to why they think they're required to have this Court re-review the evidence or reverse the decision. Within the first ground of appeal, in addition to claiming that the trial court confused motive and intent, the Prosecution also claims that the trial court believed that genocide could only be accompanied or accomplished by killing all, and I underscore "all," because I think that was the emphasis of their argument, if I'm correct, that the genocide could only be accomplished by killing all the Muslims or non-Serbs. It again refers to paragraph 553 of the trial judgement. Not surprisingly, I disagree with their analysis. Not surprisingly, perhaps, I believe that it is flawed. And not surprisingly, I would request respectfully that the appellate Chamber deny their second basis for their first ground of appeal. Perhaps after reading paragraph 553 in full, it may assist us, and I recognise we've read it before, but I think I'll make it within the time allowed by the Court, so I'd like to read it again, because now we're talking about the word "all." And if the Trial Chamber, according to the Prosecution, improperly believed that genocide could be accomplished by killing all the Muslims or non-Serbs. Again, I can start with the fourth line: "While the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the common goal of the members of the SDS in the municipality of Prijedor, including Dr. Stakic, as president of the Municipal Assembly, was to establish a Serbian municipality, there is insufficient evidence of an intention to do so by destroying, in part, the Muslim group." My emphasis is that in that very sentence, the Trial Chamber states "in part," not "all." However, the Prosecution decides that it will rely on the following language. Several lines below: "Had the aim been to kill all," underlined in the original text the word "all": "...Muslims, the structures were in place for this to be accomplished." And obviously there's other sentences within 553 that I'm not reading. The very first portion, however, of paragraph 553, which the Prosecution does not want to read, not the one that I read, but even prior to that, the preamble, if you will, of that paragraph, it states: "In relation to killing members of the group, the trial court is not satisfied that Dr. Stakic possessed the requisite dolus specialis for genocide." And it continues. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The prefatory comments by the trial court in relation to killing members does not logically coincide or support the Prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber required that all members be killed. In fact, the plain interpretation of the Trial Chamber's finding "in relation to killing members of the group," had it been, as the Prosecution alleges, an error that they wanted or required all members to be killed, they could have simply written in that first sentence, "The trial court does not say in relation to killing members or destroying members." It didn't need to use the word "members." It could have simply said to destroying groups or killing groups. The trial court, within the very paragraph that's raised on appeal by the Prosecution, on at least, in my view, two points, clearly suggests that it did not intend and did not ever apply the "all" standard to determine whether genocide should be applicable or not. All the Trial Chamber did, in my humble opinion, was to try to say: Had the aim been to kill all Muslims, the structure was in place for this to be accomplished, was to reinforce the evidence that there was no genocidal intent established, either horizontally, vertically, subordinately, or directly to Dr. Stakic. In essence, if there was an intent to destroy, according to the Trial Chamber, it could have been accomplished. The evidence and the trial court reasonably believed that no such evidence of dolus specialis was ever proven. Further, as to the second reason or claim for its first appeal, that the trial court's purported view was that genocide cannot be accomplished by killing all the Muslims and non-Serbs, the Prosecution simply ignores the trial court's decision on the specific intent to destroy a group in part, at page 140. And I have this at page 140 of the trial judgement. Each of the paragraphs listed under this section, the specific intent to destroy a group in part, does not share the view of the Prosecution in its appeal, namely, that total destruction or genocide could be accomplished only by killing all the Muslims or non-Serbs. We submit that that entire section then is misplaced in this trial judgement, if we even dare try to accept the logic or the understanding of the argument by the Prosecution. Take, for example, paragraph 522. The trial court plainly states the key factor in the specific intent to destroy the group, rather than its actual size, "size," it says, total or all or part was not of importance to the Trial Chamber. They make such an unequivocal statement, yet the Prosecution relies on one word that happened to be underlined, for whatever purpose, by the Trial Chamber. I believe it's clear, by "other portions," although as you may see later this afternoon, we do believe that the Trial Chamber was inconsistent in many aspects of their application of the law to the facts. In this instance, there was no such inconsistency; in this instance, there is absolutely not an adequate amount of evidence to establish that the trial court misapplied the standard or confused the law and unnecessarily required that all Muslims or non-Serbs be killed in order for there to be genocide. I believe, although there still might be some doubt, that the Trial Chamber made its view quite clear when it not only endorsed the Semanza - if I'm saying it correctly - trial court, in that same page 140, where we discussed where they discussed the destruction in whole or in part, when it quoted from there and said: "There is no numerical threshold of victims necessary to establish that genocide." It wasn't enough for the Trial Chamber to rely on Semanza to say: "My true intent is I don't require a numeric threshold," but the Trial Chamber then proceeds at paragraph 522 to state: "The Trial Chamber emphasises that, in view of the requirement of a surplus of intent, it is not necessary to prove de facto destruction of the group in part. It proceeds to say: "It is the genocidal dolus specialis that predominantly constitutes the crime." Although, with respect to that provision, it's my opinion, and we didn't appeal this and we're not seeking to appeal it, that that is not necessarily a correct statement of the view, a correct statement of the law, it is sufficient to utilise that provision to determine what was the Trial Chamber thinking at that time. Were they thinking "all"? Were they requiring for genocide to be found that all Muslims or non-Serbs be killed? I dare say not. But I think the Trial Chamber's judgement is unequivocal, and portions of the judgement are very clear as to the requirements of genocide and what was required. And at no time did the Trial Chamber ever state, and at no time was there any support for the proposition raised by the Prosecution as the second basis for their first appeal. Therefore, we respectfully request that the second reason or basis of the first appeal be denied and that the first ground of appeal of the Prosecution be dismissed. Now, Mr. President and members of the Appellate Chamber, the second ground of appeal that the Prosecution alleges I believe, respectfully to the Prosecution, and let me just make it clear: The Prosecution, and we have worked together, it's not an attack on them personally. I believe, quite frankly, that their position has some basis, if you will. There was the words that they cited, "rather" and "all." However, I disagree with them, and I vehemently disagree with them on these positions. And as professionals, I don't want that to be attributed to any personal disagreement, because I have none, nor any of us do with the Prosecution or its staff. However, we do, unequivocally, and very, very vehemently, disagree with their position, not only on the first ground of appeal, but the second ground of appeal, the third ground, as well as the fourth ground of appeal. Now, if we may turn to the second ground of appeal. The Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred because it found that Dr. Stakic again did not possess the dolus specialis requirement for genocide. I believe their position in this regard is misplaced, as was the first ground. The OTP claims that the Trial Chamber purportedly erred in evaluating the evidence under Article 4(2), subsection (c). So it's 4, subsection (2), (c), as I'm sure the Appellate Chamber knows. Because in essence they claim that the Trial Chamber allegedly considered only the act of deportation. We respectfully submit that the trial court did not err in its finding that Mr. Stakic did not possess the dolus specialis required for genocide for any of the reasons cited or raised by the OTP. It seems that the OTP is seeking to examine only the objective mens rea and not the subjective mens rea, as required under 4(2) of the requirement of dolus specialis. Further, with respect to the second ground of appeal, the trial court states, in paragraph 514: "The acts in paragraph (a) and (b)." I'm adding this in, obviously referred to Article 4(2): "Requires proof of a result." So the Trial Chamber clearly, in making its analysis on this second ground of appeal, or on this claim, they say that for 4(2), (a), (b), and (c), the Trial Chamber finds that with respect to (a) and (b) of Article 4(2), there must be proof of a result. It doesn't require proof of a result for 4(2)(c). The plain reading of this paragraph is that with respect to 4(2)(c): "Inflicting conditions of life," if I can paraphrase that, so that we can have a reference, that the trial court did not require proof of any result, such as deportation, subjecting the group to a subsistence diet. Systematic expulsion from homes, a denial of the right to medical services, slow deaths, excessive work or physical exertion. Not one of the resulting factors are required. Deportation, in order to prove 4(2)(c), is not required. 4(2)(c), by virtue of the language within it, does not require any result. The Trial Chamber found so again at paragraph 514, when it states: "The acts in paragraph (a) and (b) require proof of a result." Claiming that deportation is the only reason I think is misconstrued, respectfully. The Court relied on one aspect and identified it. The Court did not have to rely on any aspect, in my opinion, when it denied 4(2)(c) on the basis that there was no dolus specialis for genocide. The Court felt that as long as it found no special intent for genocide, it need not enumerate and was not required to enumerate the results necessary to accomplish 4(2)(c). In fact, at paragraph 517, the Trial Chamber specifically states that subparagraph (c): "Does not require proof of a result." In fact, it proceeds at paragraph 520: "While discussing mens rea, the Trial Chamber stressed that the acts prescribed in 4(2) of the Statute, subparagraph (a) through or to (c), are elevated to genocide when it is proved that the perpetrator not only wanted to commit those acts but also intended to destroy the targeted group in whole or in part, as a separate and distinct entity." We submit that what the OTP seems to be saying is that the objective element of actus reus should be sufficient to determine the subjective element of genocide, namely, dolus specialis. It is respectfully submitted that such an analysis would not only dilute but, in our opinion, trivialise the genocide statute. We submit that the trial court fully and exhaustively examined all the issues concerning "inflicting on the group conditions of life." The trial court again, as found at 616, that it did not believe the "conscious object of Dr. Stakic's participation in the creation and maintenance of this environment of impunity was to kill the non-Serb citizens of Prijedor municipality." In fact, at paragraphs 554, the Trial Chamber addresses the point by stating generally: "The Trial Chamber is unable to infer an intent to destroy the Muslim group." Similarly, a closer view of paragraph 557 to which the OTP is appealing opens by the prefatory remarks "for the same reasons." It is my respectful submission that this does not mean that the trial court failed to err in evaluating the evidence under 4(2)(c), but rather plainly and simply found that there was no vertical dolus specialis, no horizontal dolus specialis, no subordinate dolus specialis, and no dolus specialis relating to Dr. Stakic personally himself, as required under subsection (2) of Article 4. For the same reasons that it found no special intent for 2(a) and 2(b), the trial court found similarly no special intent for 4(2)(c). Simply put, the Trial Chamber did not need to enumerate all the acts or all the object elements which may constitute "conditions of life" in its summary. Furthermore, at paragraph 561, the Trial Chamber concludes, in our view, correctly: "On the basis of the evidence prescribed in this case, the Trial Chamber has not found beyond a reasonable doubt that evidence [sic] was committed in Prijedor in 1992." I think we have the evidence was committed in Prijedor but it's genocide, obviously. I may have misspoke, and I apologise to the Chamber. If I can just repeat that just so the record is clear. I know I'm speaking fast and I appreciate the indulgence of the interpreters. As stated in the Trial Chamber at paragraph 561, it stated: "On the basis of the evidence prescribed in this case, the Trial Chamber has not found beyond a reasonable doubt that genocide was committed in Prijedor in 1992." The Court further discusses, at 518 and 519, that being paragraphs 518 and 519, that a clear distinction must be made between destruction and mere dissolution of a group. Proving the result does not obviate or dismiss, and should not diminish the mens rea requirement of dolus specialis in genocide. Acts of destruction would not be classified as genocide unless the intent to destroy could be proven, regardless of the results achieved. Similarly, the ICTR in Akayesu, at paragraph 519, commented in the absence of an intent to destroy a protected group: "Whatever the degree ... of an act and however similar it might be to the acts described in the Convention, that act still could not be called genocide," without the necessary specific element. The trial court, it is respectfully submitted, did not apply the wrong standard and did not err in evaluating the evidence under Article 4(2)(c). Therefore, we respectfully request that the second appeal by the Prosecution be dismissed. Thank you, and excuse me. The third ground of appeal of the OTP relates to defining the target group, if you will. The OTP alleges that the Trial Chamber defined the target group too narrowly, and as a result, the Trial Chamber did not consider all the evidence it should have in determining whether Dr. Stakic had genocidal intent. We submit that indeed the Trial Chamber did fully evaluate the subjective perspective of Dr. Stakic and did not err in refusing to expand or broaden the intent of Article 4. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We've got, I think, an unedited version of yesterday's hearing, and at one point, I believe my learned colleague from the Prosecution uses some interesting words that I'd like to share with the Court. If I may. And this again, I don't have the corrected, if there were any mistakes, so I'm relying strictly on what was printed after yesterday's session. At page 48 of yesterday's appellate hearing, the Office of the Prosecution, at line 1, states at approximately 1130 and seven seconds -- let me back up, because you need this other language here. Page 47, at 1130 and two seconds, the Prosecution begins part of its argument on this third ground of appeal, and then proceeds on the next page, page 48. It states at line 25 on page 47: "So turning to the first issue," which was the third issue on appeal, "this is not a case where the Prosecution is seeking to expand the protection of the genocide convention." It goes on, of course, but for my purposes, I want to focus on that. They're saying they don't want to seek an expansion, yet in less than 20 lines after that, it uses the terms, line 16: "In a broader group, in a broader sense, an ethnic group is any group defined by ethnicity." They themselves, in my respectful opinion, within one page, tell us exactly what they want and why they're claiming that this target group was purportedly erroneously or evaluated improperly by the Trial Chamber. They are, indeed, seeking to expand and trivialise and dilute the requirements of genocide. They themselves claim that they're not seeking to expand it, but then say "we need a broader group." It is my respectful submission that the Trial Chamber did not too narrowly define the target group. It's my respectful submission that, based on the decisional authority of the ICTY and ICTR, as well as the commentary by the legal scholars on genocide, the Trial Chamber in fact correctly found not only that there was no genocide, but that the target group itself was properly defined, pursuant to the allegations alleged by the Prosecutor in their fourth amended indictment. We submit that the trial court did fully evaluate the subjective perspective of Dr. Stakic and did not err in refusing to expand or broaden the intent of Article 4. We further submit that accepting the OTP's broad construction theory would result in undesirable consequences to enlarging and thus diluting the definition of genocide. The broader and more uncertain the definition, the less of an effect it may have. Expanding the definition to "non-Serbs" or the equivalent would be a violation of the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. I never could pronounce that. It would also be a violation of in dubio pro reo as well as the Rome Statute, Article 22, subsection 2. I believe that most, if not all, the learned scholars, on the issue of narrowing or expanding genocide, such as Benjamin Whitaker, William Schabas, Pieter Drost, and Nehemih Robinson, all agree that expanding the letter and spirit of Article 4 is extremely undesirable. The Rome Statute for the ICC, as I stated, Article 22, subparagraph 2, provides that: "The definition of a crime shall be strictly construed and not be extended by analogy." The OTP is doing just that. In their example, by way of analogy, and in their argument, by way of analogy. They're doing exactly what the international criminal community, if you will, and the learned scholars have advised that we should stray away from because it will, unfortunately, present us with consequences that are not desirable. The analogy to say "all non-Serbs," would it include the Ukrainians that were in the village of Prijedor? Would it include the Russians? The Gypsies? How about during the census that was taken in the case in Prijedor? Would it include Yugoslavs, not knowing at that time if they wanted to be coined Serbs, Croats, or Bosnian Muslims? Was there even an allegation of persecution, murder, deportation, or genocide for any of those classes of people, of those ethnic groups, if you will? Of course not. There was no allegation because there was no such criminal conduct against them that would even allow them to make what we consider to be, although with some basis, a claim against Dr. Stakic. What we're saying is that you cannot broaden the target group to include a subsection of another group or a portion of that group or a sub-component of that group. The OTP relies in its argument on United States former Secretary of State Colin Powell, in order to support its expansionism theory of the target group. With respect to former Secretary of State Colin Powell, and I know his daughter went to my alma mater, so I have nothing but deep respect for him, but in this appellate argument, I dare say that at page 95 of the trial judgement, specifically, paragraph 343, when they rely on Colin Powell, this Trial Chamber, not you, but the Trial Chamber below, stated at that paragraph, while discussing Dr. Stakic's beliefs and opinions that "peace must be maintained at all costs," nevertheless found that it was "merely the typical language of a politician hiding his real political intentions." I think, in order to be fair, the Prosecution should have added that section when they relied on Secretary of State Powell. I, of course, was flabbergasted at that comment, because we working within the United Nations and the Security Council know that even the composition of this Court, with all due respect, may have some political consequences. Anything and everything we say, can that truly be considered inaccurate because we're hiding our real political intentions? We'll discuss this, hopefully, a little later this afternoon, but I couldn't help but raise it in this context. The Prosecution is relying on a politician, Secretary Powell, yet the trial judgement and the trial court below says you can never believe what these politicians say orally, because they're always hiding behind their real intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But could the counsel please kindly tell us why the comment made by the Prosecution on Secretary Powell is inappropriate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could, and I was getting to that, Your Honour. Quite frankly, and if you look at Secretary Powell, when he gave that report, he is not, obviously, a tribunal or a court of law. He did not examine all the evidence that was there. Of course, from his peripheral view, as with the Commission's report, there seems to indicate, and at least in his perspective, there seems to indicate a massive genocide that was occurring against a multitude of ethnic groups. However, that alone should not be sufficient, as the commission report alone would not have been sufficient to conclude that there was genocide. It forever would change the due process rights and international criminal law requiring principal culpability and personal, individual culpability. Secretary of State Colin Powell does assume certain facts based on the evidence presented to him. I believe that he did not make -- or his team even, did not make a specific interrogation of the adversaries in those crimes. I believe that he cannot conclude without specifically laying out with whom he interviewed, what he saw, and the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I understand. The Prosecutor yesterday, if I remember correctly, mentioned Secretary Powell's comment regarding certain acts against non-Arabs. Is that correct? Would you tell us, then -- could you analyse this a little bit why the parallel or absence of parallel with the non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I could, and I think I have in my thing. I think it would dilute the requirements of Article 4. It would expand the theory that you can say but for -- or anyone but I, is the argument that the Prosecution does. What it does, in essence, and which is the next point of my argument, because they claim that the trial court incorrectly rejected the negative analysis approach, which is what they're suggesting through Secretary of State Powell. The negative analysis approach, I believe, respectfully, not only dilutes Article 4, but it shifts the burden of proof from the Prosecution to the Defence. In fact, I believe that the approach suggested by the Prosecution would eliminate the burden of proof, and simply, someone would claim that genocide applies for everything, because it didn't apply to that defendant being accused. Would I be, and respectfully, perhaps I didn't think this through -- would I be charged with genocide because I'm taller, against all people shorter? Would that be reasonable under any circumstances? And I understand that they are required to keep it under a political, religious, and ethnic group. However, how far can we extend, by way of analogy which is prohibited by Article 22 of the Rome Statute, how far can we expand and broaden the horizons of genocide where it becomes absolutely ridiculous, in my view, respectfully, to make such an analogy? Interestingly enough, and perhaps as a segue to the next point, although I'm not done with the third point, what would the Prosecution do if a general target group were allowed and if there were a conviction found on the target group? Of course we know what they would do with respect to cumulative convictions. They would argue, I suppose, that instead of one conviction on one count, that we should have multiple convictions and then they would reverse the target group and then claim we should have a conviction for Croats, we should have a conviction for the Bosnian Muslims, and so on and so on. So their target group is in fact a moving target. It has so much elasticity that it needs, I think, to be controlled by virtue of decisional authority based upon the findings and analysis not only in this case but in the jurisprudence and in the scholarship that's written on this issue. Respectfully submitted that not only does -- that the negative approach not only shifts the burden of proof from the Prosecution to the accused, it entirely eliminates that burden of proof for the Prosecution. Furthermore, the problem, as the President has raised, I believe is specificity is required in charges and indictments, of criminal charges. Specificity in indictments, in my submission, in criminal charges will forever become vague and diluted to the extent that the presumption of innocence will be eroded and completely evaporates, and that the standard will be presumption of guilt and not the presumption of innocence, as it is today. In this case, in addition to the foregoing, the negative analysis approach unfairly redefines the elements of the protected group and respectfully dilutes and distorts the letter and spirit of Article 4. A strict, narrow interpretation is better, in our submission, not only because it ensures a fair trial, but it also prevents an abuse of process in the future. Finally, can the parts ever be greater than the whole? I respectfully think not. If the Prosecution cannot prove genocide by an allegation that a subgroup was specifically intended to be destroyed or killed, how, by coupling them together with other subgroups, can they get an enhanced theory from other crimes to the crime, the ultimate crime, as defined even by this respectful Chamber, crime of all crimes, genocide? This Honourable Appeals Chamber should dismiss the Prosecution's third ground of expanding the target group under Article 4. As I stated in my segue, they would also claim if they got a conviction on Article -- on this target group, if it was expanded, they would claim that they need to get cumulative convictions, which is their fourth issue on appeal. The fourth issue on appeal, and let me just -- because I see that perhaps the Court is somewhat confused by my argument, and I apologise. I'm saying, Your Honour, that the target group, if it's expanded, will ultimately necessitate, or ultimately the Prosecution will require that there be convictions not just on that target group, but they're going to say let's individualise and stigmatise the defendant further by holding him responsible for each subgroup of that target group, and ultimately I'm confident that they'll seek to have multiple convictions instead of just one for genocide, but multiple within this generalised target group. With respect to cumulative convictions, I believe the argument, if I understood it correctly, is that deportation and persecution should have been charged separately. I respectfully disagree. I think that this approach that's offered by the Prosecution is really an approach only to add stigmatisation and allows for the societal needs test, which, according to Blockburger, which was adopted, I believe, in this case and Celebici, where cumulative convictions were permitted, the Court examined those issues, and I believe that if you look honestly and openly at what deportation is and the requirements of deportation and the requirements required under persecution subsuming deportation, multiple or cumulative convictions on that count are not permissible and should not be allowed. I believe that the trial court, as we'll submit later this afternoon, erred in not dismissing other counts with respect to murder, which we believe is subsumed in other counts, both in persecution and in Count 3, or I think Article 3, of extermination, as was pled by the Prosecution. We believe, respectfully, Your Honours, that the duties and obligations of the Trial Chamber is not to expand and to forever find theories of liability against accused, but to evaluate the evidence that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been presented. In this case, we believe the evidence, as presented, on all four grounds of the Prosecution's appeal, clearly show that the appeal should be denied and summarily dismissed. I believe that we will raise many issues relating to cumulative convictions later this afternoon, as well as sentencing, so as to not prejudice the Prosecution - because I know we have a little bit of a break - I'll reserve my comments on that issue later. But in summary, since I have a few minutes, the first ground of appeal that the Prosecution had, they had two bases. They identify in their oral argument that they have three bases, but the third bases is really their second ground of appeal. So the first ground of appeal, confusion of motive and intent, we believe they're looking at the trial record, that that is absolutely not been proven and has not been established to a level required for appellate review. Secondly, they say that the Trial Chamber erred by requiring or evaluating the evidence and requiring that all Muslims or non-Serbs needed to be killed in order for genocide to be accomplished. Plainly, again, I believe that that's not accurate and not supported by the trial judgement or any provision within that trial judgement. Third, which is really their second argument, is the legal basis of Article 4(2)(c), and that is deliberately inflicting conditions on the group, conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part. With respect to this second ground of appeal, I think we've established, or at least I hope we have, and I'm available for this respectful Appellate Chamber to answer any questions, but result does not obviate the special intent requirement of Article 4(2)(c). And with respect to their third ground of appeal on the targeted group, I think that the decisional authority - and we cited Akayesu and other cases here, as well as legal scholarship - supports that there should not be an expansionism of genocide. And, in fact, the Rome Statute and the ICC require, as well as do statutory construction analysis, clearly require that they be strictly construed in favour of the accused and not expansively to broaden the issues. And finally, with respect to cumulative conviction, I think it's a rather straightforward analysis. I think in Kordic, I believe in this case it is a case of first impression, and despite Kordic's analysis of intra-Article 5 convictions, I believe that if you examine deportation, there are no "distinct material elements" that make a difference from persecution and that of deportation. I humbly, respectfully request that the Court dismiss the Prosecution's appeal. And thank you, Your Honours, very much for your attention to the presentation. I apologise to the interpreters for speaking perhaps too fast. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. I will ask my distinguished colleagues whether they would ask -- Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Counsel, I have one question in the framework of your submission concerning the intention to displace and intention to destroy. You advocate, as your client might, that the removal of enemy Muslims from Prijedor, rather than the physical elimination of all Muslims. But I think probably you forget or you neglect to make reference to his remark when he said: "Muslims in Bosnia were created artificially." So I would like -- do you think, in light of the term, and I emphasise again, "Muslims in Bosnia were created artificially" one can withdraw the intention to displace true intention to adjust and the intention to destroy? So it meets the intention to destroy somewhere? I would like then you to develop on this point a little further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I -- with the consent of Judge Guney, could I ask you just to wait a second, because the interpreters have to catch up. You were talking a bit fast. Mr. Registrar, you will tell me when we are ready. Counsel, you may now reply to Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, if I can, and I'll try. In all honesty, our first point is obviously it's regrettable that a man that I know personally now had ever said those words. It's clearly unfortunate, and it's shameful, quite frankly. That's not the point, and I understand it's not the point to your question. Yes, Dr. Stakic was young. That's not an excuse for that statement. Yes, he was naive politically. That is not an excuse for that statement. Yes, there was turmoil in former Yugoslavia at that time, and that's not an excuse for that statement. What our position is is when you evaluate that evidence or that statement, you have to see when it was given, when it was taken, and was it taken in the heat of the battle, as perhaps expected? Was it taken when the charges of criminal activity against Serbs was taken in that area of Bosnia? No, it was not. It was taken remotely, far away from the events of the charges against Dr. Stakic. But being that as accepted by the Trial Chamber and the Appellate Court that he did make that statement, as unfortunate as it is, we have to compare that statement, in my view, with the statements that he made contemporaneously to his position and to the acts and charges in the indictment, namely, the 30th of April to September 30th. And I must highlight for the Court that on balance, if you look at the statement that he made at an SDS Municipal Assembly meeting, that means, in my view, an assembly group that is a closely knit group that is meeting and trying to determine what was going to happen in the village of Prijedor. Dr. Stakic announces that peace should be maintained at all costs. This is in an area where he has, according to some theories of the Prosecution, absolute support. He's advocating to other constituents, to fellow colleagues, to subordinates, issues of peace. Never, I submit to the Court, did Dr. Stakic make that statement or that allegation in order to incite or encourage any participation in any criminal activity. In fact, I must say that the history of Bosnia, or Bosnia and Herzegovina and former Yugoslavia is indeed very complex. Even legal historians, quite frankly, have made that same allegation or that same claim, not in a disrespectful manner, but to say that they do not come from the Islamic states, if you will, but that they are Slavic Muslims and that they were -- this is a theory that they espouse. I don't. I haven't really looked at it in detail. But that those people were all ultimately Slavs and that they changed their religion and became Muslims. So they're saying that they adopted a religion during the Turkish Ottoman occupation of former Yugoslavia or former Kingdom of Serbia, et cetera, Croatia. So in that view, Your Honour, and it has to be placed in context, I think reliance on that one statement goes far beyond the reality of the picture, the context it was made in, when it was made, and where it was made, versus his true statements, in my view, respectfully, his true state of mind when he made statements while he was right in Prijedor, during April through September 1992. I hope I've answered the question. I'll certainly look closer to the literature to I'll see, and I'm confident, because I know I've read it, that some scholars do state, as I stated, they're not Islamic Muslims but they're Slavic Muslims. So they say the Muslim part was -- and I'm not diluting the statement. I absolutely agree that it's offensive. It's unfortunate. Obviously on behalf of Dr. Stakic, I'm sure, and I know he is, but I don't want to -- I know he regrets making that statement. It's just absolutely something that a professional that I know of Dr. Stakic's at that time should not have made in any regard. But to put it in context, if we look at it, and the reasonable inference we can draw, if he just made that statement under -- I believe it's Krnojelac, is that only if we're talking about intent, the only reasonable inference is that he's innocent, even with that statement. But I'm suggesting coupled with his other statements contemporaneous with his positions and the allegations during the time period in the fourth amended indictment that clearly is to infer that he was innocent and not that he possessed any criminal intent, much less the special, specific intent of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: A supplementary question: Don't you think that someone with high-level political authority of course statement, when one tries to wait -- with the aim to determine the intention. So the statement and the remark made by high-level, responsible of the municipality has some weight in such determination? So it is one of the ways and means when one tries to determine the intention either to displace or to destroy?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think, if I understand your question correctly, first let me say that the comment made with respect to artificially created was made in 1993, well after the time period of the fourth amended indictment. We believe that that should not have even been evidence in this case. We believe that it was done solely to prejudice Dr. Stakic, and we believe that it had actually prejudiced him, because we're still obviously discussing it. Respectfully, it's in the case, so we obviously are obligated and required to discuss it. With respect to the Court's specific question whether he stated to destroy or to displace, again, the statement, if you will, and the trial judgement has it there, Dr. Stakic's statement at one point was specific in that he said that the Muslims who shed blood against us are not welcome here, but others who left, they're welcome to return. He never, never, at least from my recollection of the evidence, ever stated that he wanted a pure Serbian municipality. Never did he advocate that, even to -- I believe it was Witness X who came to see him. Is it Witness X? Witness Z, sorry. Witness Z. When she came to visit him and he said, "I don't have the paperwork to allow you to leave the Prijedor municipality, but you probably should leave, in light of what was going on. But when you come back," when you come back, not if, not don't come back, "but when you come back, I'll help you in terms of getting your living conditions and your property or your housing," I think it was, "back to you as soon as possible." Dr. Stakic never, from those actions and from his words contemporaneous to the events, never had the intent to displace or to deport or to commit any of the crimes against these people. He did at some point, and as the Appellate Chamber respectfully knows, during a wartime, an individual as young as Dr. Stakic was at that time, when there was war, and there were paramilitary groups, and there were people which we submit in the military reports show that there was some random and sporadic violence and crimes of much lower level, of stealing and things of that sort, of course that was going on. What is someone to tell their citizens? Stay? No, leave and come back. Leave when this turmoil ends. And we believe that the reasonable interpretation of what Dr. Stakic was saying was not to kill or to destroy or to displace these people, but to save them. This is not a place where women and children perhaps should be. Please leave and come back. I respectfully believe that that was Dr. Stakic's intent at all times during this time frame, in spite of and in light of this obviously regretful statement made in 1993. I hope I've answered the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. Judge Shahabuddeen, I believe, has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I want to take you to your references to your colleague on the opposite side, seeking to expand the Convention terms. Now, is there a distinction you would say between the interpretation of a term broadly and expanding the term, the divisional line might be a subtle one, but does it exist? Is there a difference between interpreting a term and expanding the term?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to answer it this way, although I'm not a linguistics or was not a linguistic major. I believe that there is a difference, although it may fall within a similar subgroup. Similarly, not to be inconsistent, I hope you'll have an opportunity to hear our arguments of the term knowledge and awareness. We think that they are distinct. There is a distinction, quite frankly. It may be subtle. The point that I was trying to make is that if we even inch forward to expansionism, it may create undesirable consequences. So we're saying make any movement. Respectfully, obviously, that's our submission, making any movement, subtle or drastic, obviously, would not be the appropriate interpretation of the Convention Article 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What you're saying is that the Prosecution's interpretation of the Convention has the effect of expanding the Convention? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you help me on one difficulty which I have on paragraph 553, to which you have referred. You have, if I may say so, made quite convincingly the point that the Trial Chamber understood very well that the Convention speaks of the group or a part of the group. I'm with you on that. But is it possible, do you think, that the Trial Chamber might have operated on the assumption that while it is not necessary to establish an intent to kill all members of the group, it is necessary to do that in respect of a part of the group? In paragraph 553, the Trial Chamber, as you well know, uses these words: "Had the aim been to kill all Muslims, the structures were in place for this to be accomplished." You have correctly pointed out that the Trial Chamber underlined the word "all." Now, is that susceptible of a reasonable interpretation? The way the Trial Chamber looked at it was that, sure, you don't have to prove that there was a killing of all members of the group; sure, you can confine your case to a part of the group, but then you must prove an intent to kill all members of that part of the group. Is that a possible reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think, if I understand your question, although I may not have understood it, of course first I want to say that anything's possible. So, yes, of course it's possible. And then I think the Court, Your Honour, asked if it's probable. I would say no. And the reason I say no is because the trial court, if you look at their analysis on other crimes that were there, namely, extermination and their analysis with respect to murder and how they, although, with respect to genocide, reject negative analysis approach, they adopted as it relates to extermination. We'll discuss that a little later, hopefully, this afternoon. But to answer Your Honour's question, no, I don't believe that the Trial Chamber below was confused, nor, I believe, that at any time it thought that they must have killed all of the part of the group in order for there to be culpability under Article 4(2). I respectfully do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. May I turn to paragraph 616.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 616. There I should explain that I have in mind your voluble submissions on Article 4(2)(c) of the Statute. That's the one which deals with living conditions. In that paragraph, the Trial Chamber, in the third line, says this: "However, it is satisfied that Dr. Stakic, in his various positions, acted in the knowledge that the existence of such an environment would, in all likelihood, result in killings, and that he reconciled himself to and made peace with this probable outcome." Now, the outcome is probable, but he recognised the probability. Now, how does that relate to your submissions about Article 4(2)(c)? Dr. Stakic acted in that knowledge, and later on we see the Trial Chamber went on to observe that he consequently participated with the requisite dolus eventualis, and therefore incurs criminal responsibility for the killing. So the Trial Chamber is distinguishing between murder and genocide. Do you have any observations on that distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, I think. I'm not sure if they're accurate, but if the Court permits, I'll share it with all of you. I think this paragraph 616 is somewhat complicated. I think that it relates back in the first sentences of that, that it confirms what they found, that there was no dolus specialis, but the Court goes further and says that there was no special intent to kill on the part of Dr. Stakic. It goes on, I think, respectfully, to confuse, and when it uses modes of liability, with the actual crimes. So this section, paragraph 616, appears really in the extermination analysis, as opposed to the genocide analysis, I think purposefully. Secondly, I believe that the Court only reiterated it by way of summary in its first sentence that Dr. Stakic did not at any level, meaning horizontal, vertical, subordinate, as we've discussed, or to himself have a conscious object to kill. I think the Trial Chamber was hard pressed not to say that, in light of the evidence. We think that is absolutely correct, because there was no evidence that he had an intention to kill. However, then they proceeded, and regretfully they proceeded to then, in our view, use the lowest level of joint criminal enterprise and said that he had some knowledge or knowledge of it. And I think this afternoon perhaps I can more succinctly answer that. But the Trial Chamber on multiple levels, although not 121 has referred on the target group of non-Serbs, and I didn't count it, but I think in at least ten state that Dr. Stakic is aware, and I don't believe that awareness should be equated to knowledge. Here they do talk about knowledge, and I see that in there. I think the trial court was, however, wrong and erred in its application of the mode of liability in assessing that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One little supplementary question, Mr. Ostojic. You are giving me a great deal of help. I thank you. But let me put this question to you. In the first sentence in that paragraph, the Trial Chamber says: "It does not believe that the conscious object of Dr. Stakic's participation in the creation and maintenance of this environment of impunity was to kill non-Serbs, non-Serb citizens of the Prijedor municipality." Then he goes on with this. Then the Trial Chamber proceeds to make a second sentence, which I have read out. Do you think it was possible that the Trial Chamber was saying that to establish dolus specialis, the Prosecution must prove that you consciously visualise the deaths of people and that it was not enough if you acted in the knowledge that the existence of the environment was probably going to kill the people in question? So that the distinction is between, (a), a situation in which the accused consciously visualises the deaths of people; and (b), the situation which the accused has knowledge that a certain environmental situation would probably lead to their deaths? Do you think that is the way the Trial Chamber looked at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, not. I think the Trial Chamber, when they used the word "conscious object" in the first sentence, and then using the connecting second sentence, by using the word "however," I think for them, and it's clear, because it was an exhaustively written decision, that "conscious object" specifically meant both the objective and subjective intent of a crime. That's what it meant. And that's why it's in this section as opposed to in the section in genocide. I think this Court is inconsistent when it sets forth what its findings are, in my opinion, that he did not have an intent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You mean the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It's my first time appearing before the Appellate Chamber. With all due respect, I apologise for that. And I think the Trial Chamber clearly, in my view, found specifically in this section, although it exhaustively talks about other levels and the horizontal issues, subordinate, that we discussed. But here it makes an express statement that it says "the conscious object." We can define it, I think, as Websters or Oxford or any of the dictionaries. But what's the true meaning, we have to evaluate the evidence of it. And I think here the trial court properly found that he did not possess the conscious, which is both subjective and objective mens rea to kill. That's why we appealed obviously the convictions relating to killings, namely, extermination and murder, as well as persecution. And the reason I know that, or the reason I think I know it, I should say, is because I think the Court confused a lot of modes of liability and confused a lot of rather distinct and, with all due respect to the Trial Chamber, very distinct element of crimes. As we know, and I can cite to it, it confuses, I think, and will confuse in the future, if this respectful Appellate Chamber doesn't correct it, it confuses dolus specialis with discriminatory intent. They're two absolutely distinctual, and in a paragraph, in one sentence, the Trial Chamber basically says it's the same. Our resources are not as abundant, not even close, to the Prosecution. I would have appealed it, just as a matter of true, honest principles of law, not how they may apply, but that may, in other Trial Chambers, change the way other courts view it. In this case, then applying that, and I'm just trying to explain to where I'm getting to. Applying that, I think the Court here, at paragraph 616, that they were clear in their conscious object. Because if you look at the flow of the testimony and you ultimately look at the lack of testimony that was not only proffered, but the testimony that was offered at trial does not substantiate any objective or subjective mens rea for any of the crimes, I respectfully submit, and therefore the Court had but no option but to affirmatively and unequivocally state that Dr. Stakic had no conscious object to kill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I have only to thank you for your kind assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Ostojic, if I've understood you correctly with regard to the definition -- Mr. Ostojic has a slight technical problem. I'm going to wait for him to put on his headsets before I ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand correctly what you've told us, you said that the definition of the Prosecutor adopting a negative approach of the target group, you mentioned that definition of the target group of genocide and you told us that such an approach would amount to a dilution of Article 4 of the Statute. I'd be grateful -- if that's precisely what you said, I would be grateful for you to develop your argumentation on that point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will. I think the negative approach, as cited to in the Trial Chamber, referencing Jelisic specifically, says, as I think I mentioned, everyone but us. So in that analysis, as simplistic as it may seem, is what the negative approach does. So it's anyone but us, or everyone but us. So the negative approach, in essence, does not allow or permit specificity in the indictment, where the Prosecution has to say it wasn't anyone but a non-Serb or anyone but a tall person; it was actually everyone, is what they're saying, which is a negative approach analysis which I think is overly broad. I think not only does it -- as I mentioned, not only does it fail to then require the necessary specificity in an indictment, which will ultimately lead for it to be vague, I think it also shifts the burden of proof. It then becomes the burden for the accused to determine and to try to dissect whether or not there was, as alleged, any criminal intent or any criminal behaviour with respect to each of the individual groups. So I think it also shifts the responsibility of the burden of proof if all the Prosecution has to charge is to say you're a bad person with criminal intentions and your criminal conduct related to everyone. That type of negative approach, and the negative approach was properly rejected by the Trial Chamber, although respectfully, inaccurately utilised in its analysis in the extermination of provisions in this case. I think it does broaden Article 4, because then you would have people who are of a pure ethnic ethnicity or someone with pure political beliefs that you would say if you don't believe in a conservative way of thinking, it's everyone but the conservatives, or the liberals, or the moderates, for whatever the categories are in the political spectrum. Similar to race. How would you define that? Is it purely black and white? I dare say that it's not. Race is not defined purely on whether it's black or white, and it's defined, at least from my understanding, and respectfully, I hope I'm accurate on this, it includes Asians and American Indians and various other ethnic, race groups. If you allege, by way of example, that in the racial context it's non-whites, of course I believe that the negative approach by saying non-whites is to be expansive and would broaden Article 4 to a point where I think it would be useless as a tool in the criminal law jurisprudence. I hope I've answered your question. If I haven't, maybe you can direct me a little better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Vaz, do you have a follow-up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I believe that your question triggered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very small question, Mr. Ostojic. Do you have here a problem, a classical problem, of the exact relationship between the law and evidence? Theoretically, is there any reason why an accused person cannot be indicted of seeking to commit genocide in this way: He wants to set up a homogeneous state, and he says, "Everybody else who doesn't belong to that homogeneous group is slated for destruction." Now, there may be a problem. There may be a problem later on in his fitting into that non-Serb group all the components that he desires, but that's an evidential problem. Is there legally any difficulty about saying that, "I want to destroy everybody who is not a member of my particular group"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, I'm not sure if I understand or grasp the full nature of Your Honour's question. Of course, I think if someone makes that statement verbally or by actions that the law would warrant that they be charged. However, the question becomes, and as I said, actions. Had they acted upon it, and to what extent. If someone makes that statement as a purist, if you will, for lack of a better term, if they're purist in their thoughts and minds and don't act upon it, we might find them bigoted, we might find them as racist, obviously unacceptable to what we consider and what I consider to be the normal norms of society. However, if someone has those beliefs, the law, I think, does not impugn criminal culpability to him just for a belief that he desires a pure or a pure ethnic or racial state or environment. However, if he acts upon it, if he acts on those feelings, which are obviously discriminatory, in my view, I think that the criminal law and the international criminal law should and does give us some avenue or much avenue of relief that normally he should be charged and convicted, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me understand your answer to Judge Shahabuddeen. So if a leader says to his troops, "Kill everybody in my state who does not belong to my ethnic group," without more, that's the order, "kill everybody. I don't want to see anybody but our own," that would meet the definition of genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As complex as genocide is, I think more facts are necessary. However, obviously, that statement is reprehensible, and there is at least an indication that a genocidal intent is being formulated by that individual in the example. Is genocide committed? It depends on the action of the respondents to the commander or the subordinates to the commander's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If the troops start following that order, killing everybody who is outside of the ethnic group belonging to the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that. I believe that it depends -- because I believe in the Sikirica Trial Chamber's opinion with respect to the qualitative test, I believe it is, with respect to genocide. So if they do kill a majority or a qualitatively high number, yes, of course, it's genocide. If they act upon it, depending on the numbers involved, if it's far less than that specific enclave or that specific municipality, I think it's extermination. And then, as the less of the criminal activity or actions to perpetrate those crimes, I think the less, with all due respect, the less serious, although very serious, crimes, I think, would be charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. I think that you will now have 20 minutes to respond, to answer the Defence. Excuse me just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to try to respond to the points in the order that they were raised in the hearing, so it may not be a logical progression, but I'll try to address a few of the points raised by my colleague. First of all, I think it's important to note that even without the legal errors that we alleged, our basic argument in ground one is that the factual findings of the judgement, if accepted, support only one reasonable conclusion. That's addressed fully in our brief. There was no response to that argument this morning at all, and the only argument in the brief that my opponent filed on that issue is on page 25, where he says that "multiple, reasonable conclusions can be drawn from the evidence" and therefore we failed to meet our burden. He raises a number of evidentiary issues, but none of them go to the core issue of whether, if you accept all the findings of the fact as found by the Trial Chamber there was only one reasonable conclusion, and that still hasn't been addressed even this morning. There was a reference to the findings of the Trial Chamber on horizontal intent, vertical intent, subordinates intent for purposes of 7(3) liability. There was even a reference to the fact -- the discussion of complicity, that no one else was found to have genocidal intent. With all due respect, that's not relevant either. Those may be relevant to other modes of liability, but not to what was done here. And the only question was: Does he have the intent. There was some discussion, going on to the question about whether the desire was to kill all Muslims, and I'd like to respond specifically to Judge Shahabuddeen's question, because I think in your question you described exactly what it was the Trial Chamber did. And I think that's shown from the very passages that were quoted by my colleague. In paragraph 553, the Trial Chamber said: "Had the aim been to kill all Muslims, the structures were in place for this to be accomplished." Now, my colleague referenced paragraphs 522 through 526, which discussed destruction in part, and it's clear that how the Trial Chamber interpreted "in part" was to kill all individuals in a limited geographical area. And they say that in paragraph 523. They say: "In constructing the phrase destruction of a group in part, the Trial Chamber, with some hesitancy, follows the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, which permits a characterisation of genocide even when the specific intent extends only to a limited geographical area, such as a municipality." They also quote from the Krstic trial judgement, and it's curious the paragraph that they choose to quote, because it says: "Conversely, quoting from Krstic trial, the killing of all members of the group located within a small geographical area, although resulting in a lesser number of victims, would qualify as a genocide." Now, in paragraph 525, they recognise that there could be some exceptions to that, such as where the leadership of the entire group could be destroyed, but I think this passage clearly supports our interpretation of what was in the mind of the Trial Chamber when they not only said the structures were in place to kill all, but they even underlined the word "all" to emphasise what it was they meant there. On the second ground of appeal, there was some discussion about whether or not 4(2)(c) dealt with results. With all respect, our argument isn't that the question is that they didn't consider the results of the destruction, which means you don't actually have to show that people died from the conditions of life; you just have to show the conditions of life were imposed with the intent to cause death. Our argument is more on what those conditions are, not whether there were any results from those conditions. There was some discussion on the third ground of appeal. There was a reference to the comment about Secretary Powell's comment about non-Arabs. And again our argument there was not whether or not there was genocide in Darfur or not, but merely that this reflects his statement, Secretary Powell's statement represents the view of at least one leading country today on how you define genocide and the genocidal target group, and that it's appropriate to define it in negative terms, as he did, in terms of non-Arabs. I think you can actually find additional support for that, and I'd like to return to a question that President Meron actually asked me yesterday about the Nuremberg situation, which, as you know, in Nuremberg, genocide wasn't charged because the crime didn't exist yet. But genocide, nevertheless, was part of the charge as a descriptive term. And in the judgement, they found, in referencing what the intent was of the perpetrators, they said, on page 67 of the judgement: "In Poland and in the Soviet Union, these crimes were part of a plan to get rid of whole native populations by expulsion and annihilation in order that their territory could be used for colonisation by Germans. Hitler had written in Mein Kampf on these lines and the plan was clearly stated by Himmler in July 1942 when he wrote 'it is not our task to Germanise'" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: "...is to teach the people there the German language and the German law, but to see to it that only people of purely Germanic blood live in the east." That same idea was picked up in the closing argument of the British Prosecutor, Sir Hartly Shawcross, who said: "Genocide was not restricted to extermination of the Jewish people or the Gypsies; it was applied in different forms to Yugoslavia and to the non-German inhabitants of Alsace-Lorraine." So I think the idea of a negative definition actually can be traced back in some form, even to what was in the mind in Nuremberg. There was also a suggestion by my colleague that all the experts in this area would certainly not support the view of the Prosecution because genocide needs to be narrowly construed in the manner they've suggested. There are reports that I've seen, however, for example, from Samantha Powers, who has been to this Tribunal to speak and has written a leading book on genocide, who has said that Lemkin did not equate genocide with the Holocaust and the standard was never to be so high as to only mean Rwanda in the Holocaust. So I think the experts' view on this would support our position. On the same idea of expanding the group, there was a suggestion that doing it in negative terms could lead to bad consequences somewhere in the future, although I didn't hear of any bad consequences that would come from the definition in this case, the example was given that the group could be those that are too tall or are taller than me, something near to my heart, because I'm so short. I don't think in that case that would qualify, because we are not dealing with an ethnic, racial, national, or religious group. What we are dealing with in this situation is a group that is targeted because of their ethnicity, not because of their height. And they're being targeted because of the ethnicity they don't have, as opposed to the one that they do, but it's not any grounds that are improper. Finally, I'd like to address briefly, if I could, Judge Shahabuddeen's question about paragraph 616. I think it's important, first of all, to recognise that this paragraph is not placed in the judgement in the section dealing with genocide or with genocidal intent. It's intended to deal with the intent for the crime of murder. And what they found is not that Dr. Stakic did not have the intent for murder. They found that his intent was proven through dolus specialis. And therefore, he did have the actus reus and the mens rea for murder. In our submission, that's a different question about whether he had the specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part. And our support for that would be from the Jelisic appeals judgement that was delivered in July of 2005. And specifically, in paragraphs 42 and 43 of that judgement, the Prosecution had argued in that case that the Trial Chamber had erred because they had set the mens rea standard, the specific-intent standard, too high, and that they had required the Prosecution to prove that the accused must have consciously desired the committed acts to result in destruction. Consciously desired the committed acts to result in destruction. The Defence said no, that's not what the Trial Chamber found at all; all they found was that we had to prove the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. So we have to prove the intent to destroy, and that's separate from proving the crime. In that case, the Trial Chamber agreed with the Defence and found that we had misinterpreted the Trial Chamber's standard and that really all we did have to prove was the specific intent. And I think that the cases support that, that for genocide, there's two things that must be proven: You must prove that the actus reus and the mens rea for the genocidal act occurred, and then, as a separate question, you must prove the specific intent to destroy. In our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. submission, we have proven both in this case. I have no more to add on that. My colleague has a little bit to add on cumulative convictions, but I'm happy to answer any questions, if you have any more of me.
