utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall make it short. As far as the reply of the Prosecution is concerned, replying to the Defence as regards the fourth ground of appeal of the Prosecution. I would just like to make sure that there's no more confusion after the intervention of the Defence relating to cumulative convictions. Very briefly, I would like to reply and address three points. So the first relates to the indictment and the counts in this particular case. The second point relates to a finding of guilt. The third relates to the applicable law as regards the law applied by this Tribunal as concerns cumulative convictions and crimes against humanity. And the last point relates to a possible conviction by the Appeals Chamber for genocide. Now, as regards the first point, i.e., the indictment, I think we should establish a clear distinction between cumulative counts in the indictment and cumulative findings of guilt or convictions. I think the case-law is sufficiently extensive on this point as far as cumulative convictions or cumulative charges are concerned in the indictment per se. In this particular case, Milomir Stakic has been charged by the Prosecution both for persecution, Count 6 in the indictment, for murder also, Count 3 of the indictment, and lastly, for deportation, Count 7 of the indictment. I think there's no confusion as regards this particular point. My second point relates to a finding of guilt. I think it's very clear, according to the judgement, that Milomir Stakic was declared guilty as regards these three counts, i.e., persecution, paragraph 826 of the judgement, for murder, 632 and 872 of the judgement, and for deportation, paragraph 712 and 872. The Trial Chamber was to take it from there, given that it had declared Milomir Stakic guilty of these three counts, should have applied the test relating to cumulative convictions. The third point, as I have mentioned, relates to the applicable law and cumulative convictions in this case -- convictions and crimes against humanity. The Prosecution understands full well that the Defence does not appreciate the Kordic and Cerkez judgement. Nevertheless, it has to do with the applicable law in this particular case. The Defence is perfectly free and can suggest to the Appeals Chamber clear reasons in the interests of justice, paragraph 108 of Aleksovski that they move away from the Cerkez and Kordic judgement on this particular issue, but the Defence has submitted no particular argument as regards this particular issue. The parties, the Defence and the Prosecution namely, need to know with a degree of certainty which applicable law is the one that's being applied by this Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber has clearly set this out in the Cerkez and Kordic judgement. So the Appeals Chamber should rely on ratio decidendi and a prior decision, i.e., that's the principle on which the Appeals Chamber was created. And there is no valid reason which would require that the Appeals Chamber move away from the Cerkez and Kordic judgement. The question of cumulative conviction for persecution and murder is not res judicata in this Tribunal, thanks to the Cerkez and Kordic judgement. As far as deportation is concerned, according to the Prosecution, the argument put forward by the Defence lacks clarity, at the least, and the Prosecution retains its argument, i.e., that persecution and deportation contain elements that are materially distinct pursuant to the Delalic judgement. As far as my fourth point is concerned, if the Appeals Chamber grants the ground of appeal of the Defence relating to genocide, the Prosecution would then like to ask you to declare that there be cumulative convictions for crimes against humanity and genocide. This is a matter of applying the relevant case-law of the Tribunal. Krstic judgement in this particular case and Musema judgement of the Appeals Chamber. In these two rulings, the Appeals Chamber clearly stipulated that cumulative convictions for genocide and for crimes against humanity is legitimate, as it relies on the same facts. I have completed my submission, and I'm prepared to answer any questions.

Next title and ground, speculations, such as "possibly," "maybe," "I don't know," "I suppose" as a standard of proof. And the Trial Chamber accepted this as a proven fact. And you can find this text in a paragraph of trial judgement 394. Next group of our objections, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, exactly, but this doesn't fall in group 2. You don't have my papers in front of you, so it's very hard for you to follow. This is group 3, speculation is not a proper standard of proof.

utterances.text: But I follow that particular submission. You are alleging --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I divided our objections into 12 categories. The second category is regarding misquoted exhibits. The first one is regarding misquoted testimonies. The third one is regarding speculation as such "possibly," "maybe," "I don't know," "I suppose," as a standard of proof in this judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The fourth category -- all I can do now is just enumerate paragraphs, that much time I probably have. The fourth category are factual conclusions in the judgement which have no support in the evidence. Now we are in the factual conclusions. And in paragraph 5, for example, it says: "On 18 November 1990, the accused was elected to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly as the SDS deputy." And there is no base for this conclusion in the evidence in this file. And on the right-hand side in this document, I put even the exhibits and testimonies that oppose this conclusion. But even without it, it cannot stand. In paragraph 32, the same mistake. Paragraph 50, paragraph 57, 84, paragraph 153, paragraph 154, 155, 156. For example, 156, it says: "In the case of Hambarine, for the people guarding the checkpoint, to stop a car with several members of the Serb armed forces, it was clearly a defensive act. Reaction was already prepared." There is no proof in the file of the case that any kind of reaction was already proved -- prepared. Paragraph 157, the Court concluded that the announcement of the military convoy was only a provocation to justify the reaction of the military. And this factual conclusion of the Trial Chamber does not have proof in the file. Paragraph 158, paragraph 181, paragraph 182. For example, it says in paragraph 182: "The detention of the former president of the Municipal Assembly was common knowledge in Prijedor." There is no such proof in this case. And against it, testified Cedomir Vila, on transcript page 11327, and the Trial Chamber Witness Ranko Travar at 13399. Paragraph 184 says that: "This Chamber is convinced that also Dr. Stakic knew all these facts," meaning the death of Mr. Cehajic. That's conclusion without proof in this file. And eight witnesses testified that this is not true. In paragraph 343, and it was discussed this morning briefly, regarding the speech of Dr. Stakic that "peace must be maintained at all costs," the Trial Chamber found that it was merely the typical language of a politician hiding his real political intentions. And Exhibit SK46, page 2, from May 9, 1999, shows that it was a closed session of SDS Party after the takeover, with only Serbs present on this session. So Dr. Stakic should have shown his worst nationalistic face on that meeting, and on that meeting, he's telling his fellows, "We have to maintain peace at all costs." And there is no proof that this only political language hiding from whom? Only SDS members on that meeting. So we also find this is not based on any evidence, and this factual conclusion has no support in the evidence. Paragraph 344, paragraph 347, paragraph 351, paragraph 354, paragraph 367, paragraph 372, for example. The Chamber therefore finds that civilian members of the Crisis Staff wore uniforms, which provides evidence that the civilian authorities considered themselves to be on the same level as the army and the police." It was proven in this case that the members of the Crisis Staff wore uniforms for one, two, or three days after the attack on Prijedor. The Chamber's witness, Slobodan Kuruzovic, on page 14511, testified about the kind of these uniforms, and he testified that they were not real uniforms, that they are some kind of sport uniforms. But at the end, it amounted as some kind of uniform. 367 paragraph is discussing -- actually, Judge Schomburg, on page 8664, is discussing term "ciscenje," meaning mopping-up or cleansing. And this is what kind of explanation he gave us, members of the Prosecution and the members of the Defence. And military expert Ewan Brown on page 8640 also explained this term. But at the end, the Trial Chamber concluded, in 367: "In light of the foregoing, the Trial Chamber considers the term 'ciscenje' to refer to the Serb forces' conduct to round up survivors of the attacks for the detention camps and frequently arbitrarily killing them in a brutal manner under the pretext that they formed part of paramilitary groups, such as the Muslim Green Berets." And nobody ever said, and there is no trace in this file that it was done frequently or arbitrarily. There is factual conclusion in the judgement which has no support in the evidence in paragraph 375. In paragraph 471, for example: "The common goal on the Prijedor level found its vibrant expression in Radovan Karadzic's six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina which included as the first goal the separation of Serbs from the other two national communities." There is no evidence, for example, in this file that Mr. Stakic could or had seen these six strategic goals during the indictment period, the period covered by the indictment. This six strategic goals were publicised in Official Gazette of Republika Srpska in November 1993, so more than a year after the period for which Dr. Stakic was indicted. Paragraph 479, the Trial Chamber finds: "The response to the incidents at Hambarine and Kozarac in late May 1992 heralded the first in a series of measures taken by the Crisis Staff in cooperation with the military and the police, to rid the community of non-Serbs." All military documents, and we attached a list of them, but you can find them in the file of the case. And there are more than 200 military documents in this file say differently. Not a single one, not a single military document, supports this finding of the Trial Chamber made in paragraph 479. In paragraph 482, the reporting centre was located below Dr. Stakic's office in the Municipal Assembly basement, and Dr. Stakic was frequently on duty. Slavko Budimir testified that the Trial Chamber's witness, he testified on page 12912, telling that this reporting centre is under his command, that Dr. Stakic could not enter there, that he could not interfere with its work, and only professional staff was able to work in that reporting centre. It's not possible for anybody to operate in that reporting centre, which was part of the Secretariat for National Defence. And very often in this judgement we have a confusion what secretariat and what council for national defence was. Secretariat is a professional body headed by Budimir. Council is advisory by the Municipal Assembly headed by Mr. Stakic after the takeover. 482 paragraph makes the same mistake. 489. 489 is a very important paragraph for you, Your Honours, to decide. It says: "The Trial Chamber is convinced that they would have discussed the development of their common goals on such occasions. Thus, based on this mutual exchange of information, one can infer that there was an informal means of cooperation." Informal means. During the trial, the Prosecution tried to prove that there is a formal exchange of information in between Dr. Stakic's military personnel and police personnel, namely, Arsic and Zeljaja, for military, and Simo Drljaca for police. Not being successful, not having proved that such kind of exchange of information was done in between police, military and Dr. Stakic, now it's inferred that it must be some kind of informal cooperation. Dr. Stakic is not here informally. He's here because he held some official positions. That's why he was charged. And it was not proven that the formal informations were exchanged, and it was not proven that informal exchange of information was done. There is no proof in this case. There is no proof in this file, not for formal, not for informal. But probably the Trial Chamber thought it's informal, so it does not have to be proven. Still, it should have been proven, but it's not. There is no exchange of information proven in this case of any kind with military and police. Even the witnesses explained, the witnesses explained if, for example, Slavko Budimir, the Trial Chamber's witness -- it's about -- this is about acquaintances of Dr. Stakic, but I want it as exchange of information. But it's also proven that Dr. Stakic did not socialise with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Simo Drljaca and Arsic and Zeljaja outside their official duties. I have to mention paragraphs 491 to 591, 599 and 615. And I'll go to paragraph 492. You will see here, and that's what the Trial Chamber is trying all the time, it says from May 1992 he served, meaning Mr. Stakic, as a president of Prijedor Crisis Staff. It's not from May; it's from 20th of May. Those 20 days means a lot. In those 20 days -- actually, 22 days, nothing happened after the takeover. Atrocities came to happen after the military confronted armed Muslim groups, or paramilitary formations, and then everything started. For the first 22 days, before those attacks, after the takeover, nothing happened. So it's not the Crisis Staff was established in May 1992; it's on the 20th of May, 1992. And there is ample evidence. This file, for example, S180, which is Official Gazette of Prijedor municipality, talks about it. Factual conclusion made in paragraph 497 and 614, where the Trial Chamber quoted Mr. Stakic correctly, and in that quote, Dr. Stakic said: "Because we have never at any point, not even to this very day, declared war on the entire Muslim people or a struggle for the extermination of that people, but only a struggle against the extremists among that people, those who did not want coexistence here, who wanted a unitary state with absolute rights for the Muslim people and with prepared programmes for the extermination of the Serb people from these areas." The Trial Chamber, and I quote, says: "The Trial Chamber is therefore satisfied that Dr. Stakic did not differentiate between the civilian Muslim and Croat population which he claimed to want to protect against evil and harm, and the extremists, who more than anything else he wanted to defeat. In his mind, the desire for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina would qualify for being an extremist." And it's not what Dr. Stakic said here. He said "only a struggle against the extremists among that people," and there is no more blunt way to say exactly the opposite, what the Trial Chamber found. In paragraph 296, the Trial Chamber finds he knew the conditions in the camp set up in the municipality of Prijedor would not be different from those established in other parts of Yugoslavia. But the source on which Dr. Stakic was talking was newspapers, D92/92. And if he had the same kind of source for these camps, then he couldn't have known anything. And we have that S107, issued by Simo Drljaca, where he forbids for any kind of information to be revealed outside the circles of people who were inside those camps. He strictly prohibited that any kind of information would be disclosed to anybody outside of these camps. In the same category, I have 598, 599, 600, 601, paragraph 602, 604, 605, 609, 611, 612, 613, 614, 616, 629, 630, 658, 661, 707, 710, 712, 818, 819, 820, 822, 823, paragraph 824. The fifth group of documents are the documents that relate to expansion of the scope of the indictment, and according to the trial brief, it's Roman numeral I, errors by the Trial Chamber based on the expansion of the indictment. The indictment is expanded and it would be easy for you later on to check, in paragraphs number 6, paragraph number 60, paragraph number 61, paragraph number 336, paragraph number 337, 340, 341, 344, 370, 390 -- sorry, 470, 490, 492, 590, 688, 819, 917. And all those cover the period before the indictment covers. And then there is a period after the indictment, and those are paragraphs 329, 330, 331, and paragraphs 596. The sixth group of our objections has a title "Contradicting findings of fact and paragraphs in the judgement." So in the very judgement, some paragraphs and findings are contradictory to each other. The first example of that is contradiction in between paragraph 6 and 19, where it's underlined: "The Trial Chamber will discuss the events of the period between 7 January 1992 and the end of September 1992 elsewhere in this judgement, as they form part of the accused's alleged criminal conduct (including alleged preparatory acts)." In paragraph 19 it says: "Limitation of the case stems from the indictment which covers the municipality of Prijedor during a specific period, 3 April 1992 to 3 September 1992." Then, not that major discrepancy, but there is one between paragraph 66 and 117. In 66, it says: "By the end of April 1992, more than 1.500 armed men were ready to take part in the takeover." In paragraph 117, it's visible that in April there were only 453 in total of these men. Paragraph 70 and 181, it says, and that's the important one, that: "Immediately afterwards, a meeting was held at the police station. Simo Drljaca and others compiled a list of people who would be prohibited from entering the building of the Municipal Assembly," et cetera. In 181: "Dr. Stakic convened and was present at the meeting held on the evening of 29 April 1992, when the takeover was decided, and the list of persons that would not be allowed access to the important offices was written." So during this trial, we are sure that it was proven that that list was compiled as it's described in paragraph 70, not as in paragraph 181. Then paragraph 71 and 83 are contradicting. In 71, it says that the meeting, when the takeover of power was decided, was convened by Dr. Stakic, who invited the elected members of Serbian Municipal Assembly, including Simo Drljaca, Dr. Kovacevic, and Simo Miskovic to meet at Colonel Arsic's office in the JNA barracks." Until 83, a few paragraphs afterwards, it's actually Exhibit marked as S91, and the Trial Chamber states that it believes this exhibit in paragraph 83. And that audiotape and transcript, it's visibly marked as S91, that Simo Miskovic states: "Then I scheduled a meeting of the Crisis Staff for 2.00 a.m. and ordered Mr. Kuruzovic and Simo Drljaca to do the job with the army as we had agreed at the said meeting and that they were going to submit the report by 2.00 a.m." So it's contradicting who called this meeting and who was in charge of it. And there is a contradiction in between paragraph 84, on one side, and 310, 311, 312, and 313, on the other side. Then there is a contradiction in between paragraphs 123, on one side, and paragraphs 131, 576, and 609, on the other side. In 123, talking about negotiations in between army and Muslim military formations, Mirsad Mujadzic, the witness, of the Prosecution, said: "Radmilo Zeljaja issued an ultimatum calling for members of the TO to hand over their weapons." In paragraph 131, the testimonies differ on the authorship of the ultimatum, varying from the Crisis Staff and its President, Dr. Stakic, to the military authorities and even Radmilo Zeljaja. 576 says that Dr. Milomir Stakic issued an ultimatum, and 609, that attacks were ordered by the Crisis Staff. So it's obvious that there is contradiction in these paragraphs, in between them. Contradiction in between 140 and 157, 143, on one side, on the other side, 185 and 600 -- 485 and 600. It talks about the intervention platoon. (redacted), where it's established that on 26th of May, 1992, according to one of the Prosecution witnesses, this intervention platoon intervened in Kozarac. In paragraph 485, it's found that the Crisis Staff ordered, on 17th of June, 1992, so some 20 days later, that this same intervention platoon be formed. And then it also charges, in paragraph 600, Dr. Stakic with killings on the Koricanske Stijene Vlasic mountain with those killings, because Crisis Staff allegedly formed the intervention platoon 20 days after it has already been operating, according to the Prosecution witness. There is a contradiction in between paragraphs 161 and 185 regarding who organised Trnopolje reception centre. Then, on one side, paragraphs 354 and 355 are contradicting to paragraph 357. Paragraph 370 is contradicting to itself. It has -- paragraphs 373, on one side, is contradictory to paragraphs 382 and 383. For example, 373 says: "The Crisis Staff, the military, and the police cooperated with one another on the same level in order to achieve their common goals." In 382, it says -- it's one of the documents proposed by Simo Drljaca, it says: "A decision was made at a meeting of the War Presidency that the army should take over this work by 31st July 1992 and that the member of police should decrease significantly. Since the army has still not and will not take over these obligations," and it goes on. So it was for sure not anything that army listened to the Crisis Staff, and it's obvious that although the finding in paragraph 373 is that Crisis Staff cooperated at the same level with military and police, it's even clear from the statements and findings of the Court that it's not true. And in paragraph 383 underlined that: "The dispatch goes on to state that the army has refused to assume its responsibilities at the centres." This is Trial Chamber's finding. I'll skip section 7, which deals with irrelevant and immaterial events not related to Dr. Stakic. I'd like now to address for a short period of time our evidence grouped under number 9, and those are evidence which should have been deemed inadmissible. For example, in paragraph 54, or 56, and some other paragraphs, it was -- the finding of the Court is based on the report by Dr. Stakic -- sorry, by Dr. Donia, historian expert of the Prosecution. Exhibit SK42. And during the cross-examination done by my colleague, John Ostojic, this expert, at page 2111, confirmed that his expertise cannot be used in this trial. That's that bad. Because it's not maybe his fault; it's because of the documents that were presented to him. He had only a few articles from Kozarski Vjesnik, local newspapers, and when confronted with other documents, this expert says -- he was asked: "Would you agree with me, sir, that it's necessary to have a comprehensive account of these developments if someone is charged serious international crimes by virtue of actions taken by either the individual or in his capacity allegedly as an aider and abettor during that time?" "Yes, it is." "And your report is not such a report, is it?" "It is not such a report, no." So he admitted that his report is not comprehensive and cannot be used in this case. Then we think that all documents bearing, allegedly, signature of Dr. Stakic should not be admitted into evidence as well, because even the handwriting expert admitted that it's only -- you will find it on scale from 1 to 7, it's usually on a scale of 3 or 4 that something might be signed by Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Did you object during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Your Honour. We asked for another expertise. And even that expert said that: "I think that my findings should be confirmed by another expert."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think we will now break for lunch and reconvene at 2.30. But before we do so, let me return to a point I tried to clarify earlier, and this bears on the standard of review for alleged errors of fact. I referred to our standards, and I would like again to explain that the Appeals Chamber will overturn a decision by a Trial Chamber where the party alleging error has shown how a whole erroneous error of fact has caused a miscarriage of justice, as required by Article 25(b). When considering alleged factual errors, the Appeals Chamber will determine whether no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the verdict of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. We will not lightly disturb findings of fact by a Trial Chamber. Now, I believe that your mission here this morning was really to show us how the arguments you made regarding factual inaccuracies or wrong conclusions on facts, or contradictions between factual statements, had an impact, led to miscarriage of justice in this concrete case. Just by drawing our attention to what you termed "misquotations," and subsequently you changed the line to deal with perhaps "incorrect conclusions" or "inferences," you really did not help the Appeals Bench, because it is your job to show us how this would lead, in every particular case, to a denial of justice. It is not our job to do this development of the arguments for you. Now, what I would suggest to help you, during the time remaining for you this afternoon, if you would want from the materials which you presented to us this morning, if you would want to select a few where you would want to show how they lead to miscarriage of justice, make that point. Otherwise, this really does not very much help you. Now, we will reconvene at 2.30, and you will have, I believe, another hour and 30 minutes. So we will now rise. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try succinctly, and given the time frame, I'm sure I will accomplish that, to succinctly try to explain what exactly we were trying to accomplish with the binders and the issues that we raised. First, I apologise if there was confusion on that. We are alleging that the trial court, in their factual findings, were not only wrong in reaching some conclusions, but that they also misapplied certain facts and that they also unreasonably distorted certain facts, and that the inferences from certain facts were not given the standard required under the law and under the decisional authority, namely, to presume the innocence, or if an inference is to be drawn, that the inference should favour the accused or the convicted person as opposed to the Prosecution. In addition, what we were trying to show, that reliance on those facts, which we deem are extremely unreliable, for the purposes for which we suggest, that they were either misquoted, inaccurately, respectfully, distorted, that relying on those facts to the law causes an even greater miscarriage of justice. Because based on that, we feel the Trial Chamber was not able to render a just and fair verdict in this case. We outlined some of that in a somewhat different fashion for the Appellate Chamber in our brief by highlighting seven significant points. Today, if I -- or this afternoon, if I may, as we have done, I'd like to just briefly highlight three or four documents, if I can, with the assistance of our clerk here. The first one we would like to highlight is S107. It's an exhibit that has been referenced and incorporated. It goes to the issue of awareness and knowledge. I'm going to spend a few minutes today discussing those concepts with the Appellate Chamber and with your permission. S107 is a report dated May 31st, 1992, from the Ministry of the Interior, security services centre Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor. It's been our contention from the outset of this case that there has been no communication whatsoever between Mr. Stakic and people in the police and/or military. By way of example, this exhibit was offered into evidence by the Prosecution, I believe - that's why it bears the S number, if I'm not mistaken - and specifically in that document, I'd like to it highlight two things. The first page of that document in the first paragraph, it is he who signed this says: "I hereby order the following," and then he proceeds to order certain things. We think that's indicative of the type of personality that the trial court found Mr. Drljaca, or the late Mr. Drljaca to be, and also indicative of the true facts and the truth as they related in the municipality of Prijedor. Simo Drljaca was ordering certain things. He didn't go and check with anyone. He ordered them. Interestingly enough, at the third page of this document, dated May 31st, 1992, Mr. Drljaca gives a provision, on paragraph 15, on the third page -- we've tried to highlight it, if we can. And I can just read it really quickly as I'm sure the Court can examine it: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor public security station. This shall be the responsibility of the security staff." He proceeds to say in paragraph 16: "I demand most energetically that all the personnel and authorised officials in particular strictly observe these instructions. Failure to do so shall result in severe disciplinary and other measures." The point of this document is to show that indeed the information that, if any information was funnelled to Mr. Stakic, it was done in a limited fashion and that Mr. Drljaca was holding that information and not sharing that information, as other testimony will suggest. The Trial Chamber, I think, erred upon its reliance on this document to show that there was some sort of coordination. And I think it made a quantum leap of that coordination based upon this document. Now, if we take the next exhibit briefly, and I know I'm speaking fast. I apologise to the interpreters. S152, which was also a document introduced into evidence. And this depend is the same type of document. It's marked official secret, strictly confidential on page 2. I'm just going to direct the Court's attention, if I may, to page 4. But first a little background on this document. This document is a report dated August 14th, 1992, purportedly, as we've heard from other witnesses, that was given to the Banja Luka division in their hierarchy of the police. This report is the report of the trial judges -- the trial court indicated, showed that information was being given to Mr. Stakic. This report on page 4 clearly states as of August 14th, 1992 how many people perished, how many people were killed, or how many people died. Interestingly enough, this report on the very last line of page 4 states: "During" -- as he discusses the number of victims that were there and the number of various ethnic groups, et cetera, he says: "During their stay in the investigations centre, two persons, both Muslims, died of natural causes." This, for two reasons, one, it shows if we accept the Trial Chamber's view that Dr. Stakic -- or Mr. Stakic was accepting information from and getting information from the police security staff, Simo Drljaca, the question we raise and have always contested was what information was he getting? Is it enough to be aware or is it enough to have knowledge? And how much knowledge is required? Is a substantial contribution necessary or a significant participation necessary? Those are issues we hope to develop in a few minutes with the Court. Likewise, we'd like to turn your attention to a document that was introduced into evidence by the Prosecution, S407.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pages 3 and then 4, ultimately. I apologise. I'm sorry. That's the cover page, obviously, and we're trying to highlight what some of the information and to whom it was addressed. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We also wanted to show -- I know it was a little problematic in discussing reliance on misquoted exhibits, but I'd like to direct the Court's attention to paragraph 82 of the trial judgement and then compare it to S137. The Court, in paragraph 82 -- in paragraph 82 and 67 of the trial court's judgement, it discusses the dispatch sent to Simo Drljaca at the Prijedor security station to Banja Luka on April 30th. What is significant is, and I think we tried to highlight it in this, is that the Court omitted in S137, as it's reflected, omitted the words "in keeping with the conclusions reached by the Executive Committee of the Serbian assembly of the Prijedor municipality." Why is that relevant? Well, Dr. Stakic was not a member of the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of the Prijedor municipality, so this had nothing to do with Dr. Stakic. Yet by removing that, one would think, even though it lists the individuals who may have been present there, one would assume that it has some relevance to the accused. It does not, in our opinion. And what it does show is at least some examples of what we believe were errors by the trial court in determining factually the proper findings with the proper application of law, that is, that the reasonable inferences should have been afforded as to the issue of mental state. And when we're talking about mental state, we are discussing here knowledge, because in my view, there has been a dilution, and there's a lower threshold of mental state required for certain crimes, so it's that same mental state knowledge that we cannot and should not respectfully impute to Dr. Stakic. He didn't know. There is not one single witness that suggested that he informed Dr. Stakic of any killings. Now, that's all the exhibits I'd like to show, so I don't know, you may be anticipating more, but ... What I'd like to say is that the Trial Chamber not only misapplied, not only unreasonably distorted, not only failed to make the proper inferences from the facts. We believe that they completely ignored the facts, and they took the facts and somehow developed them in a manner that anything or anyone being at the wrong place at the wrong time, having the wrong ethnic composition, would be found guilty of all the crimes that were performed or accomplished in the Prijedor municipality. That's just not the case as it relates to Dr. Stakic. And I'll try to share my point with the Court. Also Vasiljevic, on paragraph 120 stated that when the Prosecution relies upon proof of the state of mind of an accused by inference, that inference must be the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. I believe that the trial court below erred and they inferred facts inappropriately, inaccurately, and therefore committed errors of law. We discussed briefly, at least we were touching upon it, the evolution of this joint criminal enterprise theory. I have had many questions about it, so I'm privileged and honoured, not that you may Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer them here, but in another session, to share some of my thoughts on that. Joint criminal enterprise, obviously, I think, has been recognised by the decisional authorities as being a judicial construct. There has been an evolution of that doctrine, and I call it a doctrine because it is a very important doctrine in criminal international jurisprudence. However, it's my submission that it can and will and was, by the Trial Chamber, respectfully, abused. Joint criminal enterprise initially, I believe, started as a common design or a common purpose. This Court answers the question: What was the common purpose or the common design relating to Dr. Stakic's involvement in the Prijedor municipality from the 30th of April through 30th September 1992? The question that is not answered directly is that the common purpose, was it criminal? The evolution went from a common purpose, determining whether it was criminal, to simply calling it a joint criminal enterprise, incorporating the word as if every common purpose, every common design, implicitly must be criminal. A very dangerous evolution in and of itself, an evolution that I believe that if we look at the findings by this Court, they never found that the common purpose or the common goal, as referred to relating to Dr. Stakic, was criminal. Yes, crimes occurred in Prijedor, horrific crimes occurred; however, the Court never answered the question: Was this common goal and this common purpose criminal? Because they state what it is and answered that it was not criminal, the common purpose that Dr. Stakic was involved in.

The common purpose to have a predominantly Serbian community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me. I thought that you started your argument on this point by referring to joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I had the impression that you started your argument on this point by referring to joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Is joint criminal enterprise discussed here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is not specifically there, but it is in other sections specifically relating to this. As we go on, I'll try to highlight it for the Court. I was in response prior to the break trying to answer in anticipation of some of the written questions and perhaps oral questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, because we wanted to be briefed on this. Please go on. Because this is, strictly speaking, not on joint criminal enterprise necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I can appreciate that, but I think the Court throughout its trial judgement, the lower court, the trial court, throughout its trial judgement makes certain statements that relate back to fundamental issues. For example, if I can highlight. The next question not only does a common goal have to be criminal, as I've tried to indicate with the common joint enterprise, the next question is whether the mode of liability which the criminal joint enterprise has been defined as being, whether that can, in and of itself, whether it be remove or strike or delete the specific elements of a crime. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, was that discussed in the context - you must help us - in the context of joint criminal enterprise, or in the context of what the Court below calls committing or co-perpetration?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think he uses the word specifically, Your Honour, joint criminal enterprise. At paragraph 437 specifically. In three sentences, this Court below --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 437. If I could read it quickly. It's three short sentences. Paragraph 437, it states: "The Trial Chamber notes with specific reference to the mens rea of joint criminal enterprise that Article 7(1) lists modes of liability only." It goes on to state, interestingly enough, and I'm in agreement with this part, that these, meaning the modes of liability, i.e., joint criminal enterprise "cannot change or replace elements of crimes defined in the Statute." It goes on to be even more specific, and it says: "In particular, the mens rea elements required for an offence listed in the Statute cannot be altered." Apparently a case of first impression. There are no citations to other jurisprudence or other courts in any jurisdiction with respect to that. I urge this Court to adopt this view and to strictly construe joint criminal enterprise that it would not, at the very beginning, so that it requires a criminal enterprise, not merely a common purpose or common design from which it evolved, but that there must be a criminal purpose to this design or enterprise. Once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you refer -- it seems that this argument is further developed by the trial court, Chamber, and just a few paragraphs below the paragraph you have quoted, paragraph 440. When we ask you to help us with stating your legal views about that, could you refer also to these paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe that what the Court did, and I respectfully submit that what the Court did is they set out appropriate legal standards and interpretation of what the joint criminal enterprise and its relationship as a mode of liability to specific crimes or any crimes are, but then it departed from that view. It abandoned that view, and in essence what it did is it stripped all accused and defendants of any and all rights that they may have in a judicial proceeding. Specifically, the Court, on paragraph 616, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, 616. Yes, Mr. President. And we've discussed this briefly today, I believe. The Court in that same paragraph states that the conscious object of Dr. Stakic was not to kill. It goes on to develop and further lower the threshold, in my opinion, of this mode of liability, joint criminal enterprise, to not only abandon the Court's prior position that you cannot change or replace the elements of intent within a specific crime. The Court in fact does that. What the Court did is say: You can't change it, but I will change it. And the Court did change it by entering the convictions. We think that's an error of law, and it's an error of fact also in its interpretation of what this lower threshold of mens rea should be. The Court cites that knowledge is that lower threshold and that joint criminal enterprise, that knowledge is significant to establish culpability under the criminal law. I humbly disagree with the Court and believe that the structures of the international criminal jurisprudence and the very foundations that it sits on will indeed be collapsed if we continue to erode theories such as mode of liability and infer from them that we can alter or replace the specific crimes, namely, the mens rea within those statutes or articles, and it will forever erode the international criminal justice system. Likewise, we see it again on paragraph 442 of the trial judgement. We see a further erosion, in my opinion, that it isn't enough to state the law than to depart from the law, to create new law, and then to further depart from that. The Trial Chamber below did just that. It went from eroding the specific intent of a crime to calling and utilising its mode of liability and saying knowledge is required. Then it proceeds on paragraph 442 to further lower the threshold of mens rea and says simply awareness or to be aware is enough to convict an individual of criminal conduct. If I can, I'd like to read the last sentence, 442. It says: "Furthermore, the accused must be aware of his own role -- that his own role is essential for the achievement of the common goal." We believe that's yet another departure and again another diluted, watered down attempt for this joint criminal enterprise theory mode of liability. Now, did the Court apply this new awareness and did it incorporate knowledge within that? We suggest, and I believe that the Trial Chamber's judgement reflects that they did not. Specifically, we asked the Court to look at the elements as they relate to Count 3 and Count 4 in the indictment, namely, extermination, as well as murder, as a crime -- crimes against humanity. Now, what I'm suggesting to the Court on paragraph 437 -- again, they set forth that you cannot change or replace the elements of a crime. Instead of applying that reasoned theory and reasoned law, the Court, in applying the critical elements of Article 3, namely, murder, nevertheless changed and replaced the elements of the crime defined in the Statute. Indeed, the mens rea for murder permitted the lower threshold of knowledge as being applicable. As we suggest, it is an error of law, both the Trial Chamber's own law and the statutory law as well. As horrific as that departure is, the Court continued, as I suggested, with respect to Count 4, to further erode joint criminal enterprise and to further erode the article and statutes which govern criminal culpability, that they require only awareness. We can look on paragraph 442 again, how the Court's mindset was in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour. Now, with respect to crimes against humanity, murder, we would direct your attention to paragraph 632, and 632, I believe, covers murder. Instead of sticking with their rulings, at 632, the Court has a one-paragraph finding as it relates to murder. And I'll read the whole paragraph for the Court. Might as well. 632, it says: "The Trial Chamber is satisfied that, in relation to those killings for which the Trial Chamber has held Dr. Stakic criminally responsible under Article 3, he is also criminally responsible under Article 5, since it finds that those killings were committed in the context of a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population of the municipality of Prijedor and..." and this is what we'd like to emphasise "...and that Dr. Stakic was aware," we would have underscored, "that his acts performed part of the attack." We went from requiring specific elements to having awareness of an attack being contemplated or performed or accomplished. Similarly, with respect to extermination, we direct the Court's attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you cite paragraph 632. There are several elements in that short paragraph. The last phrase was that Dr. Stakic was aware that his acts formed part of that attack. Are you saying that a higher degree of intention is required in relation to whether the accused appreciates that his act is almost part of the attack on the civilian population? To me it's a different thing. You have an intention to commit a crime, and then you -- the law says you must know that this crime is part of an attack on a civilian population. Do you require any extra degree of deliberation for that process of cognition?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, no, Your Honour. However, if I can explain to the Court the act or the actions here, as we've tried to argue earlier this afternoon and this morning, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. actions of Dr. Stakic was found to be as an indirect co-perpetrator. Indirect co-perpetrator, then we must examine if the rest of this sentence has any relevance to what action he may have taken with respect to any attack in the municipality of Prijedor. We dispute that there was any action. However, my arguments for today, or at least this afternoon's purposes, were strictly limited to the awareness of those actions. Of course, if someone perpetrators and is a principal perpetrator in an attack, the mens rea should not be increased; it stays where it is. The exact opposite should be true for indirect co-perpetrators and for people who do not directly commit the criminal culpable conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm interested in your arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So as I was suggesting or about to suggest, if we turn now to Article -- to Count 4 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I just continue following Judge Shahabuddeen's question. When I read paragraphs 438 through 441 of the judgement, it seems to me that the Trial Chamber, starting from the notion of joint criminal enterprise, developed an alternative vision of what happened here, in the legal sense, and preferred the view that, as co-perpetration, rather than as our classical joint criminal enterprise. And in the order which we have issued to the parties, here is the question that we posed: If the appellant's responsibility were to be analysed in terms of joint criminal enterprise, namely, not the way that the Trial Chamber did it by referring to co-perpetration but by joint criminal enterprise, would the elements of joint criminal enterprise be fulfilled based on the findings of the Trial Chamber? And the finding was co-perpetration. And we would like some guidance from you on the specific issue rather than on the abstract or otherwise definition of joint criminal enterprise. We want to know the elements of joint criminal enterprise would be satisfied or fulfilled based on the actual finding with regard to co-perpetration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At first blush, the question seems, and I believe it still is, somewhat complex, because the -- as I stated earlier, the evolution of joint criminal enterprise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If we would not think so, we would not have asked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course, I understand. I was not trying to be disingenuous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Oh, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought it was easy at first and then the more I thought of it it became a little complicated. I really believe that the joint criminal enterprise as it evolved has changed, and my opinion is somewhat changed on it. The joint criminal enterprise now has three specific, if I can call it that, three specific, different applications. The first and second, which I think the decisional authority and various scholars have referred to as the basic joint criminal enterprise, although the second one is referred from time to time as systemic, if I'm pronouncing it correctly; I think it was found in the Kvocka case as systemic, if my memory serves me correct. With respect to the first two, my answer is absolutely, unequivocally no. The facts below do not fulfil the elements which would warrant a conviction for Dr. Stakic, not whatsoever. Even if you would call him a co-perpetrator. In this case, he was found to be an indirect co-perpetrator, which has, I believe, some significant and more significant value than just merely saying a principal perpetrator and a co-perpetrator. Nevertheless, the third element which poses some problems and I was attempting not in the abstract, with all due respect to the President, but I was trying to grasp that one. The extended joint criminal enterprise, which is the one that perhaps seems somewhat troubling, but again as with the first two, I strongly do not believe that the elements of even the extended joint criminal enterprise have been fulfilled based on the evidence produced and based on the testimony that was given by all the witnesses and all the documents in this case. Now, it's easy just to say no, that it doesn't apply, obviously. Why do I think so? Because the questions, when you get to discussing a further dilution of joint criminal enterprise, which is what is happening when you go from basic to systemic to extended, is that we're bordering on a theory denounced in the criminal law practice, and that's joint -- guilt by association. Was Dr. Stakic the wrong person at the wrong time, with the wrong ethnic background? Was he that person that's being found guilty by association? We think that he is, and we respectfully think the Court erred by applying the extended joint criminal enterprise in this case, and we believe that a verdict of not guilty should have been entered based on all those facts. Now, if I can just share with the Court other -- in response to your question, we know that intent was required for basic joint criminal enterprise. I think the decisional authority requires that there be a possession of intent to commit a crime. With the systemic joint criminal enterprise, I think it's knowledge of the intent to commit the crime, and with the extended, it's merely knowledge of the crime. And we're submitting to the Chamber, to the Appellate Chamber, that the trial court further eroded that concept and merely required awareness and found on multiple occasions that Dr. Stakic was aware of the crime. The problem I have with that, respectfully, is that there is no temporal scope as to when Dr. Stakic may have known of the crime. Is it enough that we know that 500 ethnic groups, as my learned colleague from the Prosecution pointed out yesterday, are being killed and genocide is being perpetrated against them? Is that enough that we have an awareness that there will be criminal culpability? What if we were in that country? Is that enough? In this case we found, or at least I believe and we believe and submit to the Trial Chamber the awareness of Dr. Stakic, of what he knew, when he knew, are critical. The knowledge that he purportedly possessed, when he had that knowledge, and what knowledge he had, was never answered, not by the trial court, but by the Prosecution. No witness that they called came forward and said, "We told Dr. Stakic that there are atrocities happening several kilometres away, or even at your footsteps." No document, no document whatsoever, suggests that Dr. Stakic knew of the criminal activity that was being perpetrated in the town of Prijedor. We've tried to establish with some documents that in fact he was being given wrong information. We know, and we've never contested the fact that crimes, horrific as I mentioned before, occurred in Prijedor. We know that by August 12th, 1992, many of those crimes were accomplished. We know that because the international community and the Red Cross arrived in some of the camps and closed them down, and people were moved to safer places. When did Dr. Stakic become aware, or when did he know of the criminal conduct, and what specifically did he know? To be aware that an individual is a criminal is not enough. To be aware that crimes may occur in a small community or in a business district is not enough, in my view. I submit what needs to be determined is whether Dr. Stakic knew of the crimes. Did he, by virtue of his knowledge, know of their perpetration at the time it was occurring? And to what extent did he know of those crimes. Respectfully, I don't believe the evidence supports that he ever knew or that he only knew well after the periods of the indictment. The fact that a person is reckless regarding the risk is not the same as wanting the risk to realise. An argument proposed by the Prosecution is that perhaps Dr. Stakic was reckless in assuming certain risks. That would be true if we didn't have strict interpretations of statutes, and I suggest it would be true if we didn't have statutes which delineate specifically requirements for mens rea and actus reus. Did Dr. Stakic want the events that unfolded in Prijedor to occur? We suggest that there is evidence on that, and the answer is he did not. He spoke of peace. He believed in peace. And he thought that the times would change when peace would come back to that municipality. The issue of foreseeability, was Dr. Stakic able to foresee certain crimes that occurred. We heard, I believe, from testimony regarding the 200 or so men that perished in Mount Vlasic. If in the wrong place at the wrong time, perhaps many things may seem foreseeable. However, the level of foreseeability must be elevated to a higher plane, preferably to the level that the accused knew or ought to have known that the crime was committed. There is no evidence in this case to suggest that it was foreseeable, the massacre that occurred at Mount Vlasic, to Dr. Stakic. And in fact, I believe with the additional Rule 111 testimony, that it was not even known until immediately prior to the actions undertaken by the criminals who perpetrated those crimes -- 115, I meant. I'm sorry. In my submission and respectfully in my opinion, there is no other way to ensure that an innocent person or innocent persons are not wrongfully convicted of crimes over which they had no contact other than to elevate the mens rea requirement of extended joint criminal enterprise. The mens rea level of recklessness, dolus eventualis, as referred to, is far too low in the context of an armed conflict, where people are in a daily fight to save their lives, they will be reckless. Such is not a crime. I respectfully submit to the Appellate Chamber that the extended joint criminal enterprise, this third variant, if you will, of the evolution of common design and common purpose, has created a trap, a web, for anyone, as I stated, in the wrong place, at the wrong time, belonging to the wrong ethnic group, doing what is natural for such a person, and ultimately finding them liable for multiple crimes, regardless of whether that person had no substantial control of the situation whatsoever. I submit, just briefly, in summary, because I'd like to touch on two other points, if I may, the level of proof for extended joint criminal enterprise is too low. It threatens the rule of law, as innocent persons may be found guilty on very loose grounds. It makes, in my opinion, a mockery to the goal to convict the worst criminals. It makes a mockery of the noble attempts of the international criminal law and its community. Although the elevation of the level of proof may be a difficult path, and I know it's difficult when we want to change the level of proof to a higher standard, which I believe it should be, and it may lead to fewer convictions, but I believe, respectfully, that it is the only right thing to do in order to further develop an international criminal law jurisprudence that protects human rights and obligations across the world. Just briefly, and I'm not sure the time frame that I have. I'm not sure if I answered the Court's question on this point. If I may just address the other questions that the Court had. I believe I answered on the first page this morning target group of non-Serbs. If I haven't adequately, I'm available to the Chamber to try to assist to develop that further. Secondly, with mode of liability, I think the Court knows what our position is. I think it's, respectfully and humbly I'm saying this, I think it's sound, I think it's important that there be some clarity on this issue, and I think that there should not be an erosion further, in my view, of this mode of liability as it relates to crimes. This, in my opinion, again, is more significant when we relate to crimes which require distinct special intent, such as crimes against humanity, such as genocide. If we further erode and apply the third or extended joint criminal enterprise to those articles and those crimes and we erode those elements of mens rea, then I believe it will dilute and unfortunately create havoc in the international and national jurisdictions. Quickly, if I may, with respect to the Court's fifth -- sixth question relating to persecution. I started to answer it just now. The Court asks on persecution, if I may, Mr. President. May I read it? "Would the appellant still have objections to reliance on the concept of dolus eventualis within the framework of JCE? If so, what would the basis for such objections be?" My primary basis is that persecution is a crime against humanity. That article specifically requires a specific intent, that intent being discriminatory intent. It is no different from requiring an elevated mens rea that's required in Article 4 for genocide, as this different, although I believe lower threshold than the dolus specialis in genocide discriminatory intent. So because it's a specific intent crime like genocide, my objection is that you cannot have dolus eventualis. You cannot have advertent recklessness, which I believe the Trial Chamber identified it as being specifically. You cannot have that type of recklessness and then strip away the critical, distinct element of discriminatory intent pursuant to Article 5. Quickly moving along, and I know I'm close. I do have to cover Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sentencing, if the Court will just indulge me on that. I just want to answer the Court's questions on number 4, I believe, if I may again, Mr. President, just ask your question so I know I have it formulated correctly. "In the case the Appeals Chamber were to find that a necessary element of the crime of deportation is a cross-border transfer, whether such a border has to be one of the following, de jure, de facto, or three, a de facto border which has been generally recognised." My answer to that is it has to be a de jure border, that they have to specifically transfer someone to another border in order for this application for the element of the crime of deportation to apply. The third part is obviously the interesting part of the question, and that is a de facto border which has been recognised. I agree with that as well. However, we must cautiously again, when expanding provisions meaning -- I know sometimes during a war those borders become de facto and they're recognised. By whom, when, if they're recognised by the international community, then I suggest that then, and only then, can a de facto border which has been generally recognised be accepted. If we argue that de facto borders can be recognised for the crime of deportation to be held accountable for or culpable for, then I believe there will be arguments as to which state recognised you, how big or small that state may be, and what influence it may have in the international or world scene. That's why I'm hesitant to accept the de facto border which has been generally recognised, but I believe that there is some room to expand this to be a de facto border recognised, dependent upon who. If it's a United Nations-type entity that is recognising it, then yes, I believe that that's more than adequate and sufficient, in my view. I hope I've answered that. Obviously, I don't need to tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you say something about 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again: "Clarify your position concerning the mens rea of the crime of deportation with particular reference as to whether the intent of the place must be intent to the place permanently or otherwise." Yes, and I will, respectfully. I believe, and the evidence showed in this case, that Dr. Stakic never intended to displace or to deport on a permanent level. I think there's two, if not more, but at least two specific instances where Witness C, which we discussed today, in a conversation with her, and she was I think a Bosnian Muslim, if my memory is correct, and she testified when she had this conversation with Dr. Stakic, he said, "Well, come back" -- oh, yes, it's Z, as in zebra, Z, I think we say. And secondly, I think if you look at his utterances and speeches, I think there's no doubt that at any time Dr. Stakic wanted and encouraged people to come back when the trouble, the fighting, the killings in Prijedor ultimately were concluded. So in this case, I think that for a mens rea of the crime of deportation, the mens rea required is that to displace someone permanently. And I think the protections by taking this view are actually more than adequate for the criminal law jurisprudence. How so? If someone says I intend to displace you permanently, and you do that, I think it's a crime of deportation. If, in fact, that person returns, the defendant or the accused cannot suggest the person returned, therefore, I did not have the mens rea to deport them or displace them permanently. The fact that his mens rea at the time that the actual act of deportation occurred was to displace permanently, I think would still hold that individual culpable. Likewise, if the mens rea to displace permanently was not present as it was not in this case with respect to Dr. Stakic, I respectfully request and we submit that the Trial Chamber acquit Dr. Stakic of the crime of deportation as well. Your Honours, I apologise. I'm asking because I don't want to breach any rules. If I can just have a few minutes to address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If you want to sum up, I'll give you five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know that I can in five minutes, but -- I will. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If you do it in five minutes, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. Okay. Very well. Your Honour, tomorrow I'm going to address specifically sentencing, just so that the Court is aware. We believe that the evidence clear shows that Dr. Stakic was not culpable in these acts. Based on the law as it existed, based on the criminal articles and statutes that were charged against Dr. Stakic. With respect to the theory of dolus eventualis, we think that that is a complete lowering threshold of the mens rea. Applying that to crimes, such as crimes against humanity, specifically, murder and extermination, I think, respectfully, and I say this in all candour to the Court, I think that it will forever change the landscape of criminal law, not only internationally, but in national jurisdictions. I think important component parts in this Trial Chamber's judgement were touched upon, but I think the Trial Chamber failed to actually apply the very rules that they thought were logical and succinct and clear, such as replacing or -- replacing crimes -- elements of mens rea with a mode of liability. It's almost fundamental. I know the Court felt or Mr. President felt that my argument on common joint criminal enterprise was in the abstract, but I truly believe if the decisional authority does indeed show an evolution of this -- how it came about that we're using this as a mode of liability. And I apologise if I'm inaccurate on this, but I truly, from my reading of it, I thought that I was able to show this progression to some extent from common design, common purpose, to ultimately joint criminal enterprise. I believe that the evidence that the Appellate Chamber should focus on, and that is how can, in one paragraph, the Trial Chamber say he has no conscious object to kill, and then find them guilty of killings? Only by virtue of a mode of liability that is inadequate can you reach that conclusion. And it is by that leap that we object. If the crime of murder is to attempt to kill, and if the Trial Chamber found that you do not have the intention to kill, then by any mode of liability, you should be acquitted of that crime, except for the extended joint criminal enterprise, regretfully. Similarly, applying it to extermination, I believe that the Trial Chamber specifically and correctly pointed out not to replace or delete fundamental, specific elements of mens rea in the Statute, yet it did that. Extermination is a crime that requires an intent to kill. The only difference from murder is that it requires a vast amount. So you still must have the intent to kill. The Trial Chamber announced that Dr. Stakic did not have the conscious object to kill. As it relates to killing, all those counts should be, in my respectful opinion, reversed and Dr. Stakic should be found not guilty of those counts. I hope I've answered the Chamber's questions. I apologise if I have not. I'm available, if necessary, to further develop any issues the Court may deem necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel, and we are grateful for your argument and for your answers to the questions that we have addressed to you. And if I may draw your attention to the fact that some of the questions, legal questions, stated in our orders have not yet been addressed by the Prosecution. You might wish to read them. I'm terribly sorry. Judge Guney has a question for the Defence. You will have to be patient, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please, Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Before you started to sum up -- sorry. I'll repeat. Before you started to sum up, you said the mens rea requirement is that to displace someone, to displace or deport someone permanently. Could you give any specific example for the case before us, then some concrete measures were taken to show the displacement or the deportation was not permanent, was provisional? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll answer the question directly. I think I cited to two specific pieces of evidence, the Witness Z, who specifically relayed to the Prosecution and was a Prosecution witness, relayed that in fact Dr. Stakic, in my opinion, the inference did not want to displace or deport permanently by inviting her to come back. And secondly is the documentary evidence which the Prosecution again has of a tape of Dr. Stakic and various speeches that he had given, where I believe that at least one, but probably two, if my memory serves me right, stated that the Muslim community may return. And again, to answer the question directly, which I think I have, I think that the Krnojelac case is instructive because if it's unclear, and it may be unclear. Perhaps the Court doesn't accept the evidence, for whatever the reason. But if there is a doubt, that doubt should go in favour of the accused. So at worst in this case, we believe that there is enough evidence to show that Dr. Stakic did not have a mens rea for deportation because he did not want to permanently displace non-Serbs, I guess as we've called them, although I hesitate to call them that, based on my argument, but also that if we didn't have that evidence, then the facts standing alone, meaning the actions that people were deported and were displaced, did Dr. Stakic have that intent, based on no other evidence, I think that the decisional authority of the ICTR and the ICTY holds, and in Vasiljevic specifically, that that inference relating to mens rea should go towards the accused and not against the accused, in determining specifically mens rea. So I believe I've -- I've tried to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: What kind of invitation was extended to them, and when, to come back to their municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We, Your Honour, with respect to that, I have some information, just obviously being involved in the case for so long, but I don't think there's any evidence. Because the indictment is narrowly defined and there's narrow charges. The indictment ends on September 30th, 1992, so I can't really, without speculating, and I don't want to do that to my learned friend, to suggest to the Court that it was the very next day. I don't believe it was. But I believe honestly that people were returning to the Prijedor municipality later in the year 1992 and/or beginning 1993. To what extent, I honestly don't know. And I could be wrong to suggest that a few or a lot or none, but if I can just take a second to look at our case note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I guess I'm being directed to, and I apologise, to S187, and perhaps that will also be helpful to the Chamber.
