And he says -- Dr. Stakic says, I guess I'm going to read it: "Fortunately, and with great help from the international" -- this is an interview with Dr. Stakic, S187: "Fortunately, and with great help from the International Red Cross, which saw that 95 per cent of those who were in Trnopolje now, those who came later had their family homes, their apartments and told them that assistance was conditional on their return to their home. We managed to, we organised transport for them and to take them to their homes and apartments." I don't have it date on this specifically, but I think it's on 187. But because the indictment was somewhat narrow, and we did apply that, and I hope -- I appreciate that the Court will obviously read or has read our bases for alleging errors of fact and law, we believe because the indictment was so narrow, those questions were difficult and we were prohibited from trying to explore those things because I think the Trial Chamber felt that that wouldn't be an adequate defence. So we were confined to discussing anything prior to April 30th, although as we've pointed out in our brief the Trial Chamber certainly did, and to our disadvantage, and we were also prohibited from discussing anything subsequent to the 30th of September, 1992. Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And I believe that Judge Pocar was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Counsel, I was quite interested in your elaboration on the theory of dolus eventualis. In your conclusions a moment ago, you seemed to say, if I'm correct, that the theory of dolus eventualis is an acceptable lowering of the threshold of the mens rea. Are you saying that this place in regard of serious crimes or in general? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I made that statement, it was in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you are challenging in general the theory of dolus eventualis, for any kind of crimes internationally, and at the domestic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand the question now. There is a place in national jurisdictions to develop that theory of dolus eventualis as the Trial Chamber itself has cited, to German cases. However, in the international criminal law, I believe that it should not be acceptable to pick and choose various theories in order to fit what we believe an evidence should be. So to answer specifically your question, I believe that dolus eventualis can be developed in national jurisdictions, but it should not be developed in international jurisdictions unless the entire or the majority of the international community agrees to those. I mean, we've seen the discussions and the debates on even the convention on genocide, and the ultimate theories that various states tried to develop, why it should or should not include things like complicity, conspiracy, et cetera. So in that regard, I don't think we can take, even though it may be well-founded in Germany or in other national jurisdictions, respectfully I don't think we can take from that jurisdiction a certain mode of liability and apply it internationally. Because I think it would violate the principle of legality and I think it will violate also retroactive application of substantive law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So it is your view, if I understand, that the theory of dolus eventualis has been developed in some jurisdictions, but not in a number of jurisdictions sufficient to derive it as a general principle of law, whatever the denomination of the theory is, because not necessarily it's called dolus eventualis, it's a Latin expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I can answer that frankly for the Court, and I appreciate the question. I really don't know. Here's my point, though: Dolus eventualis is not, in my view, an acceptable mode of liability for international criminal conduct. That's my position in a nutshell. Whether more or fewer people think that dolus eventualis is an acceptable theory, I don't necessarily -- haven't developed the thought on that, whether if a hundred countries versus 90 countries desire it or not. Nor do I think it's consequential. What I think is more important, if I may, and that is to see whether or not that dolus eventualis actually had any impact on the actual crimes, if that mode of liability does replace, dilute, or detach any of the specific elements in a crime, such as the mens rea or actus reus or causation, then I think it's a poor use of that mode of liability, and I would suggest that it not be used anywhere, even in national jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, and this clarifies your position. I'm grateful to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, I wonder if I may put a question to you this way. You have spoken lucidly, if I may say so, about the problems which you see in any lowering of the level of normal criminal intent, especially in the case of genocide. But is there a risk of confusing the intent of the accused with the intent by which the ultimate crime may be committed? Let me explain, if I can. An accused participates in a joint criminal enterprise and he knows, when he becomes a party to the joint criminal enterprise, that there is a risk that some member of the joint criminal enterprise can commit a murder. Now, the intent of the actual murder is distinguishable from the intent of the accused. The accused only intends to participate in a joint criminal enterprise, a member of which can commit murder, and he knows that; the accused knows that. Is there any difficulty in saying that the accused is, in turn, guilty of murder?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My answer is yes. I think in the hypothetical that was offered, I believe that that would ultimately be categorised as a systemic joint criminal enterprise, the second category, also referred to as basic for some reasons in the literature. I think it would be a problem, but I think it would be further defined by identifying whether that person was in fact a co-perpetrator in that crime. And because of that, then we would have to assess, and the Honourable Court suggested that there's a risk that the murder may occur. Well, obviously that's something that needs to be assessed as well. If there was a low risk, and -- then obviously I would think less, and if there was more risk, then his intent -- then the conviction is strong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put it to you it's a real risk, it's a risk which the accused willingly accepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the accused willingly, or an accused, willingly accepts a risk, and it formulates into a systemic joint criminal enterprise, I must say that there would be criminal exposure to that accused. I honestly don't believe that there's enough facts, in all honesty, I'm not diverting it, because even in systemic as we saw in the Kordic case, I believe, they refer, and other decisional authority refers to this as concentration camp cases, which we know it is not, and I think the Chamber, the appellate chambers have clarified that issue. However, if you have only knowledge and intent of a crime, we have to go back. And I'm being very candid with the Court. You go back, and yes, if the second threshold is met, that there was intent, but then the knowledge and the appreciation of that, if, as the Court suggests, that there was a real risk or a complete appreciation of it, and absent anything else, yes, I would have to say that I would think that there would be liability in that vein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm trying to drive a distinction between the intent of the accused. He intends to participate in a joint criminal enterprise with a state of mind which accepts, which willingly accepts, that there's a risk that the murder could happen. I'm trying to separate that from the intent of the actual member of the joint criminal enterprise who commits the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My answer, respectfully, is it depends how you specifically look at the interpretation of statutory construction. If we allow the -- or the joint criminal enterprise to be evolved to a certain extent to include systemic joint criminal enterprise, then I believe the answer would be yes. My opinion, humbly and respectfully, is that it should not and that in fact that the criminal law jurisprudence, not only in national jurisdictions but internationally, is seeking to indict and convict individuals who were not only perpetrators of the crime, but obviously those that were involved in the crime to a certain degree. And to a large degree, again not to summarise in this way, but I will, Dr. Stakic, we believe, had no involvement, and there's no evidence to suggest that he did. And I say it very respectfully, without sweeping or with broad terms, we think when they talk about the knowledge or the awareness that Dr. Stakic had, we believe there's no evidence to suggest that he had that awareness and that knowledge. And the further we dilute those critical elements in the articles, I think that we will do irreparable damage and harm to the very foundations that we're working with and for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, Ms. Brady, your hour has come. And before you start, there's something that I would like you to help us with. And if you cannot answer my question today, you can do it tomorrow. You heard the argument of the Defence this afternoon. You know that the Defence submitted that the factual findings of the Trial Chamber do not support the finding of joint criminal enterprise, that Mr. Stakic was an innocent bystander in a terrible situation and that he was not basically involved. The Appeals Chamber would be greatly assisted if the Prosecution could direct us in their argument to the most egregious evidence demonstrating the involvement of Dr. Stakic in the joint criminal enterprise, as well as Stakic's relevant intent and knowledge. And if you cannot direct us to that today, you can do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, Your Honour, could I ask for two clarifications? Firstly, in relation to the Scheduling Order, the Prosecution is fully cognisant that we have two and a half hours in total to respond. In view of the lateness of the hour, can I clarify: Will we be going until 4.20 this afternoon?

utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Wait one second, please.

utterances.text: Well, I'm first very sorry. We are all very sorry to hear about the illness and wish him a very speedy and full recovery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: That would certainly suit the Prosecution very well. 4.20 or 4.30. We would be happy to finish at 4.20, and, as it were, get a credit for our time tomorrow.

utterances.text: Yes, you will get credit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. I hear that in 20 minutes we will have to change the tapes, so 20 minutes now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I'd first like to make some brief comments on the submissions that we heard this morning by Mr. Lukic before giving you an outline of how the Prosecution intends to respond to the Defence's appeal. This also makes it rather difficult for us now to respond, when we have a brief that is, according to certain grounds of appeal, 1 through 7, a much more scatter-gun approach, and we will make modifications in our response as far as we can to answer the appellant's argument and assist the Chamber. Indeed, when they referred to an error that occurred in a paragraph, they often did not identify what the error actually was. As I said, his challenges really cut across all of his grounds, and we'll attempt to deal with some specific items in the grounds as we address them. Of course, where the appellant did not amplify his arguments in the brief, there will not be a need to respond, to provide further arguments, but of course in that situation, on particular grounds, I will be available, or my colleagues, for further questions from the Bench. Now, to turn to how we're going to respond, what I will be doing now in the next 15 minutes is to give you the response of the Prosecution to ground 1, which he did touch on today. It was his grouping 5 of the errors that he referred to this morning. And to a certain extent, the errors that he touched on or addressed this morning which relate to ground 2, on procedural errors, in particular, the weight which was given to certain documents. Tomorrow we'll hear from Mr. McKeon on ground 3, followed by Ms. Goy on ground 5, dealing with murder and the threshold elements of Article 3. Then Mr. Tracol will hopefully be here, if not him, somebody else, to address you on ground 4, relating to crimes against humanity, in particular, extermination, persecution, and deportation. And, Your Honours, and this is another -- I was proposing to address on sentence, ground 6. We didn't hear any submissions on sentence today from the appellant. He did mention that he was going to raise these tomorrow. We're a bit uncertain about when he would raise them, because we don't know -- he's had his opportunity now to put his arguments in his appeal, and there would not seem a further opportunity to do so. But we're in your hands on that matter and we would have no objection if Mr. Ostojic wanted to make some submissions on sentencing. Also tomorrow, Your Honours, we would address Your Honours' remaining questions, the ones you've posed in the Scheduling Order of the 26th of September, and the one you have posed today. So with that, Your Honours, I would like to begin by addressing the appellant's arguments in relation to ground 1, which concerned the alleged wrongful expansion of the indictment, and in particular, the Trial Chamber's consideration of the pre- and post-indictment acts. This he addressed this morning in his fifth grouping of errors. In our submission, a fundamental error lies at the heart of the appellant's arguments on this ground, because, from hearing his arguments today and reading his arguments in his brief, he appears to think that he's been found guilty of a much wider temporal scope of criminal liability than he actually has. The judgement is clear that he's only liable for criminal conduct between the 30th of April and the 30th of September, not before and not after. So in other words, the Trial Chamber's finding on the expansion of - excuse me - the Trial Chamber's finding on the temporal scope of his criminal liability matched the indictment. So there's been no expansion. Simply put, the appellant Stakic was found guilty because of his own criminal conduct in the period the 30th of April to the 30th of September, as part of -- together with the co-perpetrators. And as a result of which he's criminally responsible for the persecution and extermination that occurred in that period in Prijedor. It seems that the appellant confuses the Trial Chamber's findings on his liability with the evidence and the findings used by the Trial Chamber to ascertain that liability. It's true that the Trial Chamber did consider facts and events both before and after the indictment, but not to convict him for those acts, but rather to assess whether Stakic's acts and mental state in the relevant time frame were criminal. Indeed, to bar the Trial Chamber from considering the earlier or later events would be, in our submission, completely artificial. It would be like if we were determining whether an accused is guilty of a murder committed on the 5th of October, that the fact-finder, the jury, could not consider evidence of anything that occurred before or after that day. One thing I wanted to clarify, because he made a fairly substantial argument about this in his briefs, concerning what transpired at the Status Conference on the 10th of April, 2002. According to the appellant, he says it was agreed at that Status Conference that any acts or conduct or evidence relating to the period before April 30 and after September 30 could not be considered against him. But if we go to the transcript, and in particular, the final critical exchange that occurred between the Presiding Judge and the Prosecution, we can see that this is not the case. And I'll ask if we can put a copy of that transcript on the ELMO. We can see from that exchange, and I've highlighted the critical part, which begins with Judge Schomburg saying: "Of course, one has to balance the interests I hear of the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence, and to be honest, I wouldn't regard it as a question of evidence only. It's a question for which period of time the accused is held responsible, and to prepare his own defence, I believe it's necessary." The Prosecutor responds. Ms. Korner says: "I'm sorry to interrupt. If Your Honour looks at the counts, Your Honour will see the period. That's the period, that's the period for which we're holding him liable. So between 30th of April and the 30th of September, 1992." So contrary to what the appellant submits about this, the discussion was concerning the period for which Stakic could be held liable, not the facts or the evidence which could be considered in determining that liability. This morning, Mr. Lukic referred to paragraph 6 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. He referred to it in the context of contradictory findings which he alleges can be found in the judgement. And this is the paragraph where the Trial Chamber says that it will discuss the events between the period 7 January 1992 and end of September 1992 elsewhere in the judgement, as they form part of the accused's alleged criminal conduct (including alleged preparatory acts). Now, the Prosecution can see that the phrasing in this particular paragraph is a little ambiguous. But if you look at the whole of the judgement, it's clear that the Trial Chamber did not proceed on the basis, and nor did it convict him for any earlier acts, and it restricted very carefully the temporal scope of his liability to that charged period. And I point Your Honours indeed, to the very paragraph that he referred to as the contradictory paragraph, which was paragraph 19, where the Trial Chamber specifically notes the limitations, the limits of the indictment period. I also point Your Honours to paragraph 554 and 571, when the Trial Chamber examines whether or not there's an armed conflict in existence, 627, on whether there's an attack against the civilian population; 651, when they come to examine extermination; and critically, 917, when they determine his sentence. This morning he gave some examples to show that these pre-indictment period acts should not have been considered, and in particular, I think he took issue with the paragraph 471 on the six strategic goals. Your Honour, you can see that this paragraph actually refers back to an earlier paragraph, which is 59 of the Trial Chamber's findings, in which Stakic -- or the relevance of this paragraph refers back at which paragraph 59 discusses the meeting at which Stakic was present, where the instructions from the SDS Main Board were read out. In addition, he made reference, at times very sweepingly, but to various paragraphs in paragraphs 336 to 346, concerning findings about Stakic's positions, in the earlier period, as well as his role, his significant role, in the takeover of power on the 30th of April. In our submission, the Trial Chamber cannot be considered to have been in error to examine those events in the January through April period, so that they could properly assess what he could do and did do in the relevant charge period, which is the 30th of April to the 30th of September. What the earlier findings are more or less the proper lens or the eyes with which the Trial Chamber can then properly examine the extent to which ultimately the Trial Chamber finding that he cooperated and was able to coordinate the three structures of power in the municipality, that is, the civilian, the military, and the police. Likewise, this morning he made reference to several paragraphs in the judgement which referred to what he called the later, post-indictment period events. And again, it's a similar misunderstanding being put forward. It's clear that Mr. Stakic wasn't convicted of acts which occurred after the indictment period, but, in our submission, nor was the Trial Chamber in error to consider these highly probative comments that both Mr. Stakic and the other co-perpetrators, co-perpetrators such as Simo Drljaca and Zeljaja, one of the key military figures in the area, that these people made after the indictment period. In particular, I would point Your Honours to the interviews which Mr. Stakic gave, Exhibit 187, in which Mr. Stakic refers -- is interviewed by the British -- I think it was the television crew, after the events, in which he reflects back on the extent of the cooperation between the civilian and military authorities at that time. Likewise, the later report which was made by Simo Drljaca about the camps. This particular interview, S353, the Trial Chamber actually relies on this document, it quotes this document at some length in paragraph 384, to support, it's one of the findings to support this close cooperation that the Trial Chamber found between the police and Mr. Stakic. That's all I'll say on ground 1. On ground 2, I'll just touch -- oh, I see we're at the 4.20 mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think we'll have to change the tapes now, so we'll probably call it a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: That would be suitable for the Prosecution and we'll continue our submissions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Tomorrow at 9.00 a.m., and we will now rise. Thank you, Ms. Brady, for your argument. Thank you also to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
